[Col. 0961]

EPISTOLA S. JUSTI URGELLENSIS.
AD SERGIUM PAPAM. (C,S)
chunks.english: Letter of Saint Justus of Urgel to Pope Sergius.
chunks.notes: Heading standardized for audio. The Latin abbreviation “S.” has been expanded as “Saint.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Domino meo vere piissimo, et praecipue Dei gratia
copioso, semperque in Christo beato, domino Sergio
papae, Justus episcopus.

Sciens te tam solerti studio pro refrigeriis pauperum
laborasse, ut illis temporariam consolationem,
[Col. 0961D] tibique acquisieris aeternam mercedem, et jam satis
te dijudicans totum ad Dei eloquia, ex quibus nunquam
fuisti vacuus, pro animae cultura converteris;
quoddam tibi in corporali specie spiritale exenium
dirigere procuravi; quod si tibi Christus non ex nostro
merito, sed ex suo munere fecerit esse gratissimum,
[Col. 0962B] forsitan proveniet, et in diebus jejunii quodammodo
refectus ad mensam venies, et antequam cibum
accipias quiddam praegustasse persenties. Nec hoc
dicens transmissionis hujus meritum, priusquam approbes,
arroganter insinuare studeo; sed intercedente
charitate, in qua te totum possideo, ita de tuo tanquam
de meo animo praesumens, tibi acceptum fore
absque ulla ambiguitate confido. Igitur in Christo
Jesu germanum cordis mei esse non nesciens libellum
de tractatu libri canonici qui Cantici Canticorum
praescribitur, quem nuper Christo illuminante edidimus,
tibi primum censui offerendum. In quo non
nostra potius, sed ea quae tua sunt, quia sic diligitis,
te suscepisse cognoscas: quem precor ut cum ea sollicitudine
qua in Christo viges, saepe recenseas: ut
si quid illic corrigendum persenseris, integra libertate
[Col. 0962C] commoneas. Et sic caeteris in Christo fratribus
relegendum, vel si fortasse placuerit offeras transcribendum.
Itaque quia sic accidit ut membranis desistentibus,
minutioribus litteris eamdem scripturam,
in paribus quaternionibus susciperent, nec studiose
fabrefactis lateralibus ambiretur; si memoratam rem
alicujus meriti esse censueris, quia hoc ipsum, ut
praefatus sum, donante Domino, tuum est, ut diligentiori
studio transcriptum utilius coaptetur quantocius
studebis. Quod opus si laude dignum processerit, te
auctorem referam Christo; si vero reprehensioni patuerit,
quia utriusque est, statim assumam socium
temetipsum, quia decori sic te condecet haec quae
Deus contulit coaptari, ut non de negligentia vituperium,
sed de industria charitatis suscipias fructum:
[Col. 0962D] ut fratres nostri qui praecessorum Patrum tractatibus
epulantur, etiam his neotericis quae eis ex charitate
offerimus, non pro nostro merito, sed pro Dei dono
et sua benevolentia vesci quodammodo delectentur.
Ave nunc in Christo, piissime, nostramque pusillitatem
sanctis orationibus in Domino fove.
chunks.english:
To my truly devoted lord, especially rich in the grace of God, and always blessed in Christ, the lord Pope Sergius: from Justus, bishop.

I know how diligently you have worked to bring relief to the poor. You have gained temporary comfort for them, and eternal reward for yourself. And judging that you have now turned yourself sufficiently and wholly toward the words of God, from which you have never been empty, for the cultivation of your soul.

For that reason, I have taken care to send you a spiritual gift under a physical form. If Christ makes it very pleasing to you—not because of any merit of ours, but by his own gift—then perhaps this will happen: even during the days of fasting, you will come to the table already refreshed in some way, and before receiving food you will feel that you have tasted something in advance.

By saying this, I am not arrogantly trying to recommend the value of what I am sending before you have approved it. Rather, because love stands between us—and in that love I possess you wholly—I presume upon your mind as I would upon my own, and I trust without any doubt that it will be acceptable to you.

Therefore, knowing that you are a brother of my heart in Christ Jesus, I decided that I should offer first to you this little book, a treatment of the canonical book called the Song of Songs, which we have recently produced by Christ’s illumination. In receiving it, please understand that you are not so much receiving what is ours, but what is yours, since you love such things.

I ask you to read it over often, with the careful attention by which you flourish in Christ. If you notice anything there that needs correction, please point it out with complete freedom. And then offer it to the other brothers in Christ to read over, or, if it should perhaps please you, to copy.

Now, because it happened that parchment was lacking, the same work was written in rather small letters, gathered into equal quires, and not surrounded with carefully prepared margins or outer presentation. So, if you judge the work to have any value—and as I said, by the Lord’s gift this very thing is yours—please see as soon as possible that it is copied with greater care and arranged in a more useful form.

If this work turns out to deserve praise, I will tell Christ that you are its author. But if it lies open to criticism, then, since it belongs to both of us, I will immediately take you yourself as my partner. For it is fitting to your dignity that the things God has given should be properly arranged, so that you receive not blame for negligence, but the fruit of love’s diligent work.

Then our brothers, who feast on the writings of the earlier Fathers, may also take pleasure in being nourished, in some way, by these more recent works that we offer them out of love—not because of our merit, but because of God’s gift and their own goodwill.

Farewell now in Christ, most devoted father, and support our littleness in the Lord with your holy prayers.
chunks.notes: “Refrigeria pauperum” means practical relief or refreshment for the poor. “Exenium” is a gift, here deliberately described as spiritual despite its material manuscript form. “Papa” (rendered “Pope”) is here the honorific of Sergius, metropolitan bishop of Tarragona, not the bishop of Rome.

chunks.chapter_title: The Church Longs for Christ’s Kiss
chunks.latin:
CAPUT PRIMUM.

[Col. 0963A]
chunks.english: Chapter 1: The Church Longs for Christ’s Kiss.
chunks.notes: “CAPUT PRIMUM” has been standardized as “Chapter 1,” with a descriptive title drawn from the first interpretation that follows.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 1. Osculetur me osculo oris
sui. Vox Ecclesiae haec est venientis ad Christum in
osculo; offensam quam apud Deum homines peccando
contraxerant resolvi cupientis, et pacem in qua,
dum essemus Deo Patri inimici, per ipsum Filium
ejus reconciliamur, invenire desiderantis: propter
quod propheta ad Deum: Pacem tuam, Domine, da
nobis, et omnia reddidisti nobis (Isa. XXVI) . In Evangelio
quoque (Luc. XV) redeuntem a regione longinqua
filium pater deosculatus est. Tunc enim quodammodo
venientibus ad se osculum tradidit, quando
unicum suum in homine nasci voluit, per quem etiam
ut ei pacis vinculo adhaereamus attribuit. Denique et
angeli, nascente Christo: Gloria in excelsis Deo, et in
terra pax hominibus bonae voluntatis (Luc. VIII) , idcirco
[Col. 0963B] voce consona clamaverunt, quia ipsum qui est pax
nostra nobis utique talia dicendo, perspicue docuerunt.
chunks.english:
The first verse says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is the voice of the Church as she comes to Christ for a kiss. She wants the offense removed—the offense that human beings had incurred before God by sinning. She longs to find peace: the peace in which, while we were enemies of God the Father, we are reconciled through his Son.

For this reason the prophet says to God, in the book of Isaiah, chapter twenty-six: “Lord, give us your peace, for you have given everything back to us.”

And in the Gospel of Luke, chapter fifteen, the father kissed the son who returned from a far country. In a certain sense, God gave this kiss to those who came to him when he willed that his only Son should be born as a human being. Through that Son, God also granted that we might cling to him in the bond of peace.

Finally, when Christ was born, the angels cried out together, as the Gospel of Luke, chapter eight, is cited here: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” They cried this because, by those words, they clearly taught us that Christ himself is our peace.
chunks.notes: The quoted angelic hymn corresponds to Luke chapter two, though the printed text cites Luke chapter eight.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 2. Quia meliora sunt ubera tua vino, flagrantia
unguentis optimis. Ubera Christi, apostolos, evangelistas
non incongrue accipimus; per ipsos enim in
fide nutrimur et spirituali alimento reficimur. Idcirco
autem meliora vino probantur, quia evangelica doctrina
eminentior quam lex olim data dignoscitur.
Denique illic figura, hic veritas; illic tanquam austeritas
vini diligendum tantummodo proximum et inimicum
odiendum ostendit, hic dulcedo gratiae pro
inimicis orandum, et eos qui nos oderunt admonet diligendos.
Ipsa quoque Christi ubera, id est apostolos,
unguentis optimis flagrantia declarat, quia tantis virtutibus
[Col. 0963C] tantisque enituere miraculis, ut odor justitiae
eorum longe lateque diffusus tunc intuentes oblectaret,
et usque huc omnes reficiat audientes, sicut unus
ex ipsis pronuntiat dicens: Deo autem gratia, qui
semper triumphat nos in Christo Jesu, et odorem notitiae
suae manifestat in omni loco pro nobis (I Cor. II) .
chunks.english:
The text continues: “For your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.”

By Christ’s breasts, we may fittingly understand the apostles and evangelists. Through them we are nourished in faith and refreshed with spiritual food.

They are shown to be better than wine because the teaching of the Gospel is recognized as higher than the law given long ago. There, in the old law, was figure; here, in the Gospel, is truth. There was something like the sharpness of wine: it showed that one should love only one’s neighbor and hate one’s enemy. Here there is the sweetness of grace: it tells us to pray for our enemies and to love those who hate us.

The text also says that Christ’s breasts—that is, the apostles—are fragrant with the finest ointments. This means that they shone with such great virtues and such great miracles that the scent of their righteousness, spread far and wide, delighted those who saw them then and refreshes all who hear them even now.

As one of the apostles declares, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter two: “Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus, and for our sake makes known in every place the fragrance of the knowledge of him.”
chunks.notes: The wording of the quoted Pauline passage corresponds more closely to Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter two, though the printed text cites Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter two. The printed text reads “pro nobis” where the Vulgate has “per nos”; the translation follows the printed reading.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 3. Oleum effusum nomen tuum, ideo adolescentulae
dilexerunt te. Quem unxit Deus, id est Christum,
oleo laetitiae, prae participibus suis (Psal. XLIV) ,
hujus etiam velut oleum effusum est nomen: quicunque
enim Christiani a Christo nominantur ipsique
chrismate perunguntur, atque in ejus nomine baptizati
sancto Spiritu adimplentur, ut unguentum quod
descendit a capite in barbam Aaron (Psal. CXXXII) ;
quod verum, perfectum, atque fortissimum declarat;
[Col. 0963D] id est sacer Spiritus, qui a Deo diffusus est in Christo,
descendit etiam in oram vestimenti ejus, ac totam,
usque in finem, Ecclesiam replet; quae ei inhaerendo,
sine dubio vestis ipsius est. Nam in transfiguratione
[Col. 0964A] vultus ejus splenduit sicut sol, ut in Evangelio
legimus, et indumenta ipsius velut nix candida facta
sunt (Mat. XVII; Luc. IX) , quae talia nullus fullo super
terram facere potuit. Nullus enim doctorum ad tantum
nitorem sicut ille discipulos suos aliquando perduxit;
vel sic a maculis ablutos, instar nivis candidos in se
credentes facit. Hunc ergo adolescentulae, vel novellae
Ecclesiae vel incorruptae animae dilexerunt; quae
etiam flagranti unguento repletae cum Apostolo dicunt:
Charitas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris per
Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis (Rom. V) .
chunks.english:
The text says: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women have loved you.”

God anointed this one—that is, Christ—with the oil of gladness above his companions, as Psalm forty-four says. Therefore his name also is like oil poured out. All who are called Christians take their name from Christ. They are anointed with chrism, baptized in his name, and filled with the Holy Spirit.

This is like the ointment that descends from the head onto Aaron’s beard, as Psalm one hundred thirty-two says. That ointment signifies what is true, perfect, and most powerful: the Holy Spirit. The Spirit, poured out by God upon Christ, descends even to the edge of his garment and fills the whole Church to the very end. And because the Church clings to Christ, she is without doubt his garment.

For at the transfiguration, as we read in the Gospel, Christ’s face shone like the sun, and his clothing became white as snow. The printed source cites the Gospel of Matthew, chapter seventeen, and the Gospel of Luke, chapter nine. No fuller on earth could make clothing like that. For no teacher has ever led his disciples to such brightness as Christ has, nor has anyone else so cleansed those who believe in him from stains and made them white like snow.

Therefore the young women loved him. These young women are the new churches, or uncorrupted souls. Filled with this fragrant ointment, they say with the Apostle, in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter five: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”
chunks.notes: “Adolescentulae” is interpreted allegorically as newly formed churches or pure souls.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 4. Trahe me post te, curremus in odorem. Dicit
Dominus in Evangelio: Nemo venit ad me nisi Pater,
qui misit me, attraxerit eum (Joan. VI) . Attrahitur
enim ad Christum qui credit in Christo; illi vero currunt
[Col. 0964B] post eum, qui eum imitantur vel qui dono ipsius
ipsum sequendo proficiunt.
chunks.english:
The text says: “Draw me after you; we will run after your fragrance.”

The Lord says in the Gospel of John, chapter six: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

A person is drawn to Christ when that person believes in Christ. But those who run after him are those who imitate him, or those who, by Christ’s own gift, make progress by following him.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 5. Introduxit me rex in cellaria sua. Introduxit
Christus Ecclesiam in sua cellaria, cum ei revelavit
Scripturarum occulta mysteria, sicut Apostolus
ait, ut ostenderet in saeculis supervenientibus abundantes
divitias gratiae suae in bonitate super nos in
Christo Jesu (Ephes. II) . Vel tunc ex toto sancti introducuntur
in Christi cellaria, cum eis in fine dicetur:
Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod
vobis paratum est ab origine mundi (Matth. XXV) .
chunks.english:
The text says: “The king has brought me into his storerooms.”

Christ brought the Church into his storerooms when he revealed to her the hidden mysteries of the Scriptures. As the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two, God did this “so that in the ages to come he might show the abundant riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.”

Or, in another sense, the saints are brought completely into Christ’s storerooms when at the end it will be said to them, in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-five: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”
chunks.notes: “Cellaria” can mean inner rooms, storerooms, or wine cellars. Justus interprets them as the hidden riches of Scripture and, ultimately, the kingdom.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 6. Exsultabimus et laetabimur in te memores
uberum tuorum super unum. Exsultant sancti et laetantur
in Domino, cum recordantur quemadmodum
per ubera Christi, apostolorum scilicet doctrinis, spirituali
[Col. 0964C] lacte nutriti sunt. Quam doctrinam Christi
dum priscae legis praeceptis inspiciunt clariorem, in
illa vel ex ipsa Christum intuentes intelligunt, quibus
ipse in Evangelio dicit: Vestri beati oculi qui vident,
et aures quae audiunt; amen dico vobis, multi prophetae
et reges quaesierunt videre quae videtis, et non viderunt;
et audire quae audistis, et non audierunt (Matth. XIII;
Luc. X) .
chunks.english:
The text says: “We will rejoice and be glad in you, remembering your breasts more than wine.”

The saints rejoice and are glad in the Lord when they remember how they were nourished with spiritual milk through the breasts of Christ—that is, through the teachings of the apostles.

And when they perceive that Christ’s teaching is brighter than the commandments of the ancient law, they understand it, beholding Christ in that teaching and from it. To them he says in the Gospel: “Blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear. Amen, I say to you: many prophets and kings desired to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it.” The printed source cites the Gospel of Matthew, chapter thirteen, and the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten.
chunks.notes: The printed lemma reads “super unum”; the translation follows the Vulgate “super vinum” (“more than wine”), which the exposition presupposes.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 7. Recti diligunt te. Nec enim pravi possunt
diligere aequitatem: illi enim recti sunt et diligunt
Deum, qui non amore creaturae captivi tenentur; sed,
sicut rectos decet, pretiosum munus praeponentes,
Deo auctori omnium dilectione fortissima adhaeserunt.
Sed et illi Deum recte diligere approbantur, qui non
solum in beneficiis, sed in flagellis ipsius constituti,
[Col. 0964D] similiter gratias agunt sicut et ille dicebat: Benedicam
Dominum in omni tempore, laus ejus in ore meo
(Psal. XXXIII) : id est, et quando laetitiam ex dono capio,
et quando dolorem (eodem corripiente) suscipio.
[Col. 0965A] Sicut alius quoque vehementissima passione probatus,
carne putridus, et sincerus corde locutus est:
Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini, mala cur non
sustineamus? Dominus dedit, Dominus abstulit, sicut
Domino placuit ita factum est; sit nomen, etc.
chunks.english:
The text says: “The upright love you.”

The crooked cannot love righteousness. Those are truly upright, and truly love God, who are not held captive by love for created things. Instead, as is fitting for upright people, they set the precious gift first and cling with the strongest love to God, the maker of all things.

Those also are proved to love God rightly who give thanks in the same way not only when they receive his benefits, but also when they are placed under his chastisements. One such person said in Psalm thirty-three: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth.” That means: I bless him both when I receive joy from his gift, and when I receive pain as he corrects me.

Likewise another man, tested by an extremely violent suffering, with his flesh diseased but his heart sincere, said: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things? The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.”
chunks.notes: The final quotation combines language associated with Job’s responses in the book of Job, chapters one and two. The Latin ends with “etc.,” indicating the continuation of the familiar biblical phrase.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 8. Nigra sum, sed formosa, filia Jerusalem, sicut tabernacula Cedar. Nigra confessione peccatorum, formosa gratia sacramenti, filia Jerusalem. Ex illa enim primitivorum Ecclesia per Evangelium nata est quae prima credidit in Jerusalem; vel certe, sicut Apostolus dicit: Illa quae sursum est Jerusalem, libera est, quae est mater nostra (Galat. IV) . Et merito, quia assimilat se tabernaculis Cedar; quod interpretatur, obscuritatis; ad cujus filios Apostolus dicit: Fuistis aliquando tenebrae, nunc autem lux in Domino (Ephes. V) . Potest etiam nigra vocari, cum passionibus, opprobriis, contumeliis et despectui traditur. Considera nigram atque formosam: in Paulo: In omnibus tribulationem patimur, sed non angustiamur; aporiamur, sed non destituimur; dejicimur, sed non perimus (II Cor. IV) . Quemadmodum tabernacula Cedar; tanquam purgamenta hujus mundi facti sumus, omnium peripsema; et sicut pellis Salomonis, semper mortificationem Jesu Christi in carne nostra circumferentes, ut vita Jesu manifestetur in carne nostra mortali.
chunks.english: The bride says: “I am dark, but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar.” She is dark through the confession of sins, but beautiful through the grace of the sacrament. She is a daughter of Jerusalem because she was born through the Gospel from that first Church, the Church of the first believers in Jerusalem. Or, as the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter four: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.” And rightly so, because she compares herself to the tents of Kedar; Kedar means “darkness.” To Kedar’s children the Apostle says, in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter five: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.” She can also be called dark when she is handed over to sufferings, insults, abuse, and contempt. Look at how she is both dark and beautiful in Paul’s words, in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter four: “We suffer tribulation in every way, but we are not crushed; we are at a loss, but not abandoned; we are struck down, but we do not perish.” She is “like the tents of Kedar” because, as Scripture says, “we have become like the refuse of this world, the scum of everyone.” And she is like “the curtains of Solomon” because, in the Apostle’s words, we are “always carrying around in our body the death of Jesus Christ, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our mortal flesh.”
chunks.notes: “Kedar” is interpreted here as “darkness.” The phrase “scum of everyone” echoes Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter four, verse thirteen, though the Latin does not cite it explicitly. The printed lemma has the singular “filia Jerusalem” (Vulgate “filiae”), which the exposition follows; the translation keeps the singular.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 9. Nolite me considerare quod fusca sim, quia decoloravit me sol. Id est: nolite me constitutam in persecutione despicere; aestus enim tribulationum sustinui, et quasi decorem temporalis jucunditatis amisi: Per multas enim tribulationes oportet me intrare in regnum Dei (Act. XIV) . In illis namque sum de quibus scriptum est: Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolabuntur: et vos quidem tristitiam habebitis, mundus autem gaudebit, sed tristitia vestra in gaudium convertetur (Matth. V; Joan. XVI) .
chunks.english: She says: “Do not stare at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me.” That means: do not despise me because I have been placed in persecution. I have endured the burning heat of tribulations, and I have, as it were, lost the beauty of temporary happiness. As Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter fourteen: “Through many tribulations I must enter the kingdom of God.” I belong among those of whom it is written in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter five: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” And again, in the Gospel of John, chapter sixteen: “You will indeed have sorrow, and the world will rejoice; but your sorrow will be turned into joy.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 10. Filii matris meae pugnaverunt contra me. Filii scilicet Synagogae, qui docentem et arguentem Stephanum martyrem lapidaverunt: Et facta est persecutio magna in Ecclesia quae erat Hierosolymis, et omnes fratres dispersi sunt per regiones Judaeae et Samariae (Act. VII) . Vel illi etiam pugnaverunt adversus Ecclesiam, qui Paulum praedicantem in gentibus, per civitates singulas persecuti sunt. Similiter et illi qui his qui ex gentibus crediderant, onera legis imponenda censebant, quae B. Jacobus cum caeteris apostolis salubriter removenda decrevit (Act. V) . Nam et illi qui Galatas in Christo credentes circumcidi suaserant, perturbantes evangelicam traditionem adversus Ecclesiam pugnasse docentur, de quibus Paulus apostolus ait: Neque enim hi qui circumciduntur legem custodiunt, sed volunt vos circumcidi ut in carne vestra glorientur (Gal. V) . De ipsis etiam dixit: Utinam abscindantur qui vos conturbant (Ibid.) .
chunks.english: She says: “The sons of my mother fought against me.” That is, the sons of the Synagogue fought against her: those who stoned the martyr Stephen while he was teaching and rebuking them. As Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter seven: “A great persecution arose against the Church in Jerusalem, and all the brothers were scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria.” Or this may also refer to those who fought against the Church by pursuing Paul from city to city while he was preaching among the Gentiles. Likewise, it includes those who thought the burdens of the Law should be imposed on believers who came from the Gentiles—burdens which blessed James, together with the other apostles, wisely decided should be removed, as the Acts of the Apostles, chapter five, records. And those who persuaded the Galatians who believed in Christ to be circumcised are also shown to have fought against the Church, because they disturbed the evangelical tradition. About them the Apostle Paul says, in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter five: “Even those who are circumcised do not keep the Law; they only want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.” And about the same people he also says, in the same passage: “I wish those who are troubling you would cut themselves off.”
chunks.notes: The Latin cites the persecution after Stephen under Acts chapter seven, but the quoted line is from Acts chapter eight. The reference to the apostolic decision about Gentile believers is better associated with Acts chapter fifteen, though the Latin gives Acts chapter five. The first Galatians quotation is from chapter six, verse thirteen, though the Latin gives chapter five.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 11. Posuerunt me custodem in vineis. Vineae quoque istae, Synagogae sunt: Acceperat quippe Saulus potestatem, et epistolas a principibus sacerdotum, ut quoscunque credentes in Christo reperisset viros ac mulieres, in custodias tradere ut punirentur (Act. XI et XXII) : ut dum ista perpetraret, quasi Synagogae vineam custodiret. Et sequitur, Vineam meam non custodivi. Factus enim ex Saulo Paulus, ex persecutore praedicator, dum verbum Dei Judaeis contradicentibus praedicaret et omnino sperneretur, eisdem incredulis dixit: Vobis quidem oportebat praedicari verbum Dei, sed quoniam repulistis illud et indignos vos judicastis tanta salute, ecce convertimur ad gentes, sic enim praecepit nobis per Scripturam Dominus: Dedi te in lucem gentium, ut sis in salutem usque ad extremum terrae (Act. XIII; Isa. XLIX) . Vel sicut ipse ad Galatas scripsit, Audistis conversationem meam in Judaismo, quia persequebar Ecclesiam Dei, et expugnabam illam et proficiebam in Judaismo supra multos coaetaneos meos in genere meo, abundantius aemulator existens paternarum mearum traditionum (Gal. I) . Et iterum: Sed quae mihi fuerunt lucra, haec arbitratus sum detrimenta (Philip. III) , tanquam sub aenigmate dicens: Posuerunt me custodem vineis, vineam meam enim non custodivi.
chunks.english: She says: “They made me keeper of the vineyards.” These vineyards are the synagogues. Saul had received authority and letters from the chief priests so that, if he found any men or women who believed in Christ, he could hand them over to prison and punishment, as the Acts of the Apostles, chapter eleven and chapter twenty-two, relate. While he was doing this, he was, in a sense, guarding the vineyard of the Synagogue. Then the bride adds: “But my own vineyard I did not keep.” For Saul became Paul, and the persecutor became a preacher. When he preached the word of God to the Jews, and they contradicted him and utterly rejected him, he said to those unbelievers, as told in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter thirteen: “It was necessary that the word of God should be preached to you first. But since you have rejected it, and judged yourselves unworthy of so great a salvation, behold, we turn to the Gentiles.” For the Lord commanded us through Scripture, in the book of Isaiah, chapter forty-nine: “I have made you a light for the Gentiles, so that you may be salvation to the ends of the earth.” Or, as Paul himself wrote in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter one: “You have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how I persecuted the Church of God and tried to destroy it, and how I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, being far more zealous for the traditions of my fathers.” And again, in Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter three: “But whatever things were gains for me, these I have considered losses.” In this way Paul speaks, as if under a figure: “They made me keeper of the vineyards, but my own vineyard I did not keep.”
chunks.notes: The Latin references Acts chapters eleven and twenty-two for Saul’s authority to persecute Christians; the narrative is primarily in Acts chapter nine, with Paul’s later retelling in Acts chapter twenty-two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 12. Indica mihi quem diligit anima mea, ubi pascus, ubi cubas in meridie. Legimus in Evangelio: Si dixerint, Ecce hic est Christus, ecce illic, nolite exire (Matth. XXIV; Marc. XIII) . Hic enim atque illic, partes esse noscuntur; Christus autem in Ecclesia catholica tanquam in meridie cubans, mundum universum suo fulgore perfudit, et in spiritu ferventibus requiescit, atque ex ea charitate qua orbem universum irradiat, credentes in se populos quotidie pascit.
chunks.english: She says: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture your flock, where you lie down at noon.” We read in the Gospel: “If they say, ‘Look, here is Christ,’ or, ‘Look, there he is,’ do not go out.” That warning appears in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-four, and in the Gospel of Mark, chapter thirteen. For “here” and “there” indicate divided parties. But Christ rests in the catholic Church as at noon: he has flooded the whole world with his brightness, he finds rest in those who are fervent in spirit, and from the love by which he illumines the entire world, he daily feeds the peoples who believe in him.
chunks.notes: “Catholic” is used here in its ancient sense: the universal Church, spread throughout the whole world.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 13. Ne vagari incipiam per greges sodalium tuorum: id est, si in ea claritate qua fidelium tuorum universitas consistit, te habitantem ignoravero, per greges sodalium, id est per congregationes haereticorum, incipiam oberrare. Sodales quippe Christi ex quadam parte haeredici appellentur, quia nativitatem, passionem, et resurrectionem ipsius profitentur; sed quia de ipsis Apostolus ait: Habentes formam pietatis et virtutes ejus abnegantes (II Tim. V) , non jam sodales, sed adversarii comprobantur.
chunks.english: She says: “Do not let me begin to wander among the flocks of your companions.” That is: if I fail to recognize that you dwell in the brightness where the whole community of your faithful people stands, then I will begin to stray among the flocks of your companions—meaning, among the gatherings of heretics. Heretics can, in one respect, be called companions of Christ, because they confess his birth, his passion, and his resurrection. But because the Apostle says of them, in Paul’s second letter to Timothy, chapter five, “They have the outward form of godliness, but deny its power,” they are proven to be not companions any longer, but opponents.
chunks.notes: The Latin citation gives Second Timothy chapter five, but Second Timothy has no chapter five; the quotation is from Second Timothy chapter three, verse five. The Latin appears to have a scribal form “haeredici” for “haeretici,” meaning heretics.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 14. Si ignoras te, o pulcherrima inter mulieres, egredere et abi post vestigia. Vox Christi est ad Ecclesiam, Si ignoras te, o pulchra inter mulieres: si non intelligis quia tu es illa cui in psalmo dicitur: Audi, filia, et vide, et inclina aurem tuam, et obliviscere populum tuum et domum patris tui, quia concupiscit rex pulchritudinem tuam (Psal. XLIV) , quia tu sola accepisti decorem incorruptibilis sacramenti. Et bene ait, inter mulieres, id est, gloriosa inter haereses: congrue enim mulierum nomine vocitantur, quia virginitatem quae est in Christo amiserunt. Igitur non oberres, me alibi extra te quaerendo ullo modo; in te quippe ubi me hactenus non quaerebas, tanquam in meridie requiesco. Jam intellige ubi me pascentem et gubernantem temetipsum quaeras, ne velut in nocte quorumlibet simulatio te abducat: quia tantummodo in te certa sinceritas me apud te regnante perdurat, in illis te esse cognosce, quibus post resurrectionem meam veraciter repromisi: Ecce ego vobiscum sum usque ad consummationem saeculi (Matth. XXVIII) . Quod si quadam promissorum meorum dubitatione aliquo modo fluctuas, nec meam praesentiam, nec tuam pulchritudinem cognoscis: egredere, et abi post vestigia gregum tuorum. Merito etenim post vestigia gregum perget, quia pastoris praesentiam dereliquit. Et pasce haedos tuos juxta tabernacula pastorum: injustos homines oblectans traditionibus vel conventiculis haereticorum. His etenim redargutionibus objurgari merentur, qui Christum in catholica Ecclesia, vel seipsos Ecclesiam catholicam esse non cognoscunt.
chunks.english: Christ speaks to the Church: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and follow the tracks.” This is the voice of Christ to the Church: “If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women”—if you do not understand that you are the one to whom it is said in the Psalms, psalm forty-four, “Listen, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house, because the king desires your beauty,” since you alone have received the beauty of the incorruptible sacrament. And he rightly says, “among women,” meaning: glorious among the heresies. For the heresies are fittingly called “women,” because they have lost the virginity that exists in Christ. So do not wander by looking for me anywhere outside yourself. I rest within you, where until now you were not looking for me, as though at noonday. Now understand where you should look for me as the one who feeds and governs you, so that the imitation practiced by others does not carry you away as if into the night. Since sure sincerity endures only in you, because I reign within you, know that you belong among those to whom, after my resurrection, I truly promised in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-eight: “Behold, I am with you until the completion of the age.” But if you waver in doubt about my promises, and recognize neither my presence nor your own beauty, then “go out and follow the tracks of your flocks.” Such a person rightly follows the tracks of the flocks, because she has abandoned the presence of the shepherd. And “feed your young goats beside the tents of the shepherds”—that is, delight unjust people with the traditions and little assemblies of the heretics. These rebukes are deserved by those who do not recognize Christ in the catholic Church, or who do not recognize that they themselves are the catholic Church.
chunks.notes: The psalm cited as psalm forty-four corresponds to psalm forty-five in many modern English numbering systems.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 15. Equitatui meo in curribus Pharaonis. Dicit Abacuc propheta: Nunquid in fluminibus iratus es, Domine, aut in fluminibus furor tuus, vel in mari indignatio tua, qui ascendis super equos tuos, et quadrigae tuae salus (Abac. I) ? Quos equos, apostolos et evangelistas accipimus? Ideo Christus loquitur ad Ecclesiam. Tunc equitatui meo in curribus Pharaonis assimilavi te, cum sapientes mundi ad meam fidem evocandos converti, ut deposito tumore saeculi, sub me (qui sum salus vera) currendo proficiant; meque circumferendo piis praedicationibus, credentium fide oculis manifestent. Ac sicut princeps mundi hujus qui jam missus est foras, falsis philosophis tanquam claris curribus usus est ad perniciem, ita ego mea sapientia repletis apostolis, credentes instituam ad salutem.
chunks.english: He says: “I have compared you to my cavalry among the chariots of Pharaoh.” The prophet Habakkuk says, in the book of Habakkuk, chapter one: “Were you angry with the rivers, Lord? Was your wrath against the rivers, or your indignation against the sea, when you mounted your horses, and your chariots were salvation?” We understand these horses to be the apostles and evangelists. Therefore Christ says to the Church: I compared you to my cavalry among the chariots of Pharaoh when I turned the wise people of this world, calling them to my faith. I did this so that, once they had laid aside the swelling pride of the age, they might make progress by running under me, for I am true salvation. By carrying me through devout preaching, they would make me visible to the eyes of believers through faith. And just as the ruler of this world, who has now been cast out, used false philosophers like splendid chariots for destruction, so I, through apostles filled with my wisdom, will train believers for salvation.
chunks.notes: The Latin cites Habakkuk chapter one, but the quotation is from Habakkuk chapter three. “The ruler of this world” echoes the Gospel of John, chapter twelve, verse thirty-one.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 16. Pulchrae sunt genae tuae sicut turturis. Castitatem comitem verecundiae praedicavit. Dicitur enim genus turturum amisso corporali consortio solitarium incedere, nec carnalem copulam ultra requirere. Habet itaque Christi sponsa eximiam pulchritudinem, quando cum pudore retinet castitatem.
chunks.english: He says: “Your cheeks are beautiful, like those of a turtledove.” He is praising chastity as the companion of modesty. For it is said that turtledoves, once they have lost their bodily mate, go about alone and do not seek another physical union. So the bride of Christ possesses exceptional beauty when she preserves chastity together with modesty.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 17. Collum tuum sicut monilia. In collo hi insinuantur qui legem Dei diebus ac noctibus meditari non desistunt, quique etiam velut munda animalia, salutarem doctrinam jugiter ruminando reddunt. Hi, quia praeclara Ecclesiae ornamenta sunt, velut sponsae monilia describuntur.
chunks.english: He says: “Your neck is like necklaces.” The neck signifies those who never cease to meditate on the law of God day and night, and who, like clean animals, continually chew over and bring forth saving doctrine. Because such people are splendid ornaments of the Church, they are described as the necklaces of the bride.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 18. Murenulas aureas faciamus tibi. Vox ista doctorum est, qui tunc ornamenta Ecclesiae auro argentoque permixta disponunt, quando spiritales intelligentias eloquii nitore disserunt. Murenulae autem a capite defluentes, solent ad cervicem ornandam aptari: et idcirco illae doctrinae praeclarae sunt, quae a capite, id est Christo, procedentes, sic spirituali officio ministrant, ut cervicem nostram jugo Christi subdendam edoceant, ita ut talibus ab Apostolo dicatur: Non alta sapientes (Rom. XI) , etc.
chunks.english: The speakers say: “Let us make little golden chains for you.” This is the voice of the teachers. They arrange ornaments for the Church, mixed with gold and silver, when they explain spiritual meanings with the brilliance of eloquence. These little chains flow down from the head and are normally fitted to adorn the neck. For that reason, those teachings are truly excellent which proceed from the head—that is, from Christ—and serve in such a spiritual way that they teach our neck to submit to the yoke of Christ. To such people the Apostle says, in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eleven: “Do not set your mind on high things,” and so on.
chunks.notes: The wording “Do not set your mind on high things” is closer to Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter twelve, verse sixteen, though the Latin gives chapter eleven.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 19. Dum esset rex in accubitu suo. Narrant Evangelia (Marc. XIV; Joan. XII) , ante biduum Paschae, recumbente Domino, a muliere habente alabastrum unguenti nardi pistici ejus capiti superfusum, et hic prophetia dicit: Cum esset rex in accubitu suo, nardus mea dedit odorem suum. Igitur tam haec quam illa figurate dicta vel facta noscuntur, quia Rege nostro (vel in cruce ubi inclinato capite spiritum reddidit, vel in sepulcro ubi corpore conditus requievit) in suo accubitu constituto, Ecclesia piae confessionis odorifero unguento eum perunxit, ut cum voluntarie passum fuisse, et a mortuis resurrexisse die tertia virtute propria, in salutem credentium praedicare non cesset.
chunks.english: “While the king was on his couch.” The Gospels tell us—in the Gospel of Mark, chapter fourteen, and the Gospel of John, chapter twelve—that two days before the Passover, while the Lord was reclining at table, a woman who had an alabaster jar of pure spikenard ointment poured it over his head. And here the prophecy says, “While the king was on his couch, my spikenard gave forth its fragrance.” So both the prophetic words and the Gospel event are understood figuratively. For when our King was in his own place of rest—either on the cross, where he bowed his head and gave up his spirit, or in the tomb, where his body was laid and rested—the Church anointed him with the fragrant ointment of a faithful confession. She did this so that she might never cease to proclaim, for the salvation of believers, that he suffered willingly and rose from the dead on the third day by his own power.
chunks.notes: The Latin citation compresses the Gospel traditions: Mark describes the anointing shortly before Passover; John places a related anointing in Bethany before Passover. The printed text reads “ut cum voluntarie passum fuisse” for “ut eum …” (him); the translation follows the evident sense.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 20. Fasciculus myrrhae dilectus meus. Myrrhae species, mortuorum corporibus condiendis apta dignoscitur. Fasciculus itaque myrrhae Christus passus et mortuus et sepultus. Inter ubera mea commorabitur. Ubera Ecclesiae esse eruditi et spirituali lacte redundantes qui nascentes in fide populos nutriunt, illi sine dubio comprobantur, qui mortem Domini, sicut praeceptum est, annuntiare donec veniat, omnibus modis non desistunt.
chunks.english: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh.” Myrrh is known as a spice suitable for embalming the bodies of the dead. So Christ is the bundle of myrrh: Christ who suffered, died, and was buried. “He will remain between my breasts.” Those who never stop proclaiming the Lord’s death in every way, as they have been commanded, until he comes, are without doubt proved to be the breasts of the Church: learned teachers who overflow with spiritual milk and nourish the peoples being born in the faith.
chunks.notes: The final phrase echoes Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse twenty-six.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 21. Botrus Cypri dilectus meus. Botrus in Cypro, Christus suspensus in crucis ligno: quod genus ligni odoriferum semper et incorruptum est, signum etenim crucis, cum odore chrismatis praenotamus in fronte. Bene autem ait: Botrus Cypri, dilectus meus mihi, quia non illis qui crucifixerunt, sed his qui in crucifixum crediderunt, botri istius dulcedo concessa est. In vineis Engaddi; in Synagogae populis, ubi dominica peracta est passio. Engaddi interpretatur oculus tentationis meae. Lege Evangelium, et invenies Pharisaeos et Sadducaeos nihil aliud intendisse suis interrogationibus, nisi ut Dominum per singula tentarent, et invenirent causas accusandi cum; quibus ipse dicit: Quid me tentatis, hypocritae (Matth. XXII) ? Sed tantum bonum passionis Christi, illis quidem gestum, nobis autem qui credidimus constat esse concessum.
chunks.english: “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus.” The cluster in the Cyprus tree is Christ hanging on the wood of the cross. That kind of wood is always fragrant and incorruptible; and indeed, with the fragrance of chrism, we mark the sign of the cross on the forehead. He rightly says, “My beloved is a cluster of Cyprus to me,” because the sweetness of this cluster was granted not to those who crucified him, but to those who believed in the Crucified One. “In the vineyards of Engaddi” means among the peoples of the Synagogue, where the Lord’s passion took place. “Engaddi” is interpreted as “the eye of my testing.” Read the Gospel, and you will find that the Pharisees and Sadducees aimed at nothing else with their questions except to test the Lord at every point and to find grounds for accusing him. To them he says, in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-two, “Why do you test me, hypocrites?” Yet the immense blessing of Christ’s passion, though carried out among them, is clearly granted to us who have believed.
chunks.notes: The Song’s phrase often refers to henna blossoms or Cyprus; Justus interprets it through the wood of the cross and the fragrance of chrism. The printed text reads “causas accusandi cum” for “eum” (him); the translation follows the evident sense.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 22. Ecce tu pulchra es, amica mea. Christus Ecclesiam, quam amicam pacis suae osculo fecit, bis pulchram pronuntiat, sicut Apostolus sanctam corpore et spiritu (I Cor. VII) esse docuit, adjiciens, oculi tui columbarum. Nihil est magis quod faciem ornet in corpore quam dispositio oculorum, per quos convenienter sanctos apostolos accipimus, qui etiam futura prospicere potuerunt; quorum privilegia designans beatus Paulus apostolus ad Corinthios scribens ait: Vos estis corpus Christi (I Cor. XII) . Et alio loco: Quosdam quidem posuit Deus in Ecclesia primum apostolos (Ephes. IV) , etc. Jam cum dicit, oculi tui columbarum, ipsos apostolos, quibus praeceptum est ut essent astuti sicut serpentes, et simplices sicut columbae (Matth. X) , evidenter ostendit: per cujus avis similitudinem, eosdem sancto etiam Spiritu repletos esse demonstrat.
chunks.english: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend.” Christ calls the Church beautiful twice, because by the kiss of his peace he has made her his friend. In the same way, the Apostle teaches, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter seven, that she is holy in body and in spirit. Christ then adds, “Your eyes are like doves.” Nothing adorns the face of a body more than the proper placement of the eyes. By these eyes we rightly understand the holy apostles, who were even able to look ahead to future things. Describing their privilege, the blessed apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter twelve, “You are the body of Christ.” And in another place, in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter four, he says that God has appointed certain people in the Church, first of all apostles, and so on. So when Christ says, “Your eyes are like doves,” he is clearly pointing to the apostles themselves. They were commanded, in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter ten, to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. And by comparing them to this bird, Christ also shows that they were filled with the Holy Spirit.
chunks.notes: The Latin cites Paul's letter to the Ephesians, chapter four, for the appointment of apostles, but the wording more closely matches Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, chapter twelve, verse twenty-eight; Ephesians chapter four contains a related list of ministries.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 23. Ecce tu pulcher es, dilecte mi. Christum, quem pulchrum et decorum Ecclesia hoc loco commemorat, Psalmista sic pronuntiat, dicens: Speciosus forma prae filiis hominum, diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis (Psal. XLIV) . Sed haec tua pulchritudo exinde est, quia In principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum; et Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis (Joan. I) . Addens autem, lectulus noster floridus, ipsum corpus dominicum in quo Deitas requievit, sincerum odoriferum, ex Virgine natum ostendit.
chunks.english: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.” The Church here calls Christ beautiful and lovely, and the Psalmist proclaims the same thing when he says, in Psalm forty-four, “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured out on your lips.” But your beauty, Christ, comes from this: as the Gospel of John, chapter one, says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; and again, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Then the Church adds, “Our little bed is flowering.” By this she points to the Lord’s own body, in which the Godhead rested: pure, fragrant, and born from the Virgin.
chunks.notes: Psalm forty-four in the Latin numbering corresponds to Psalm forty-five in many modern English Bibles.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 24. Tecta domorum nostrarum. Domus istae in quibus Christus habitat, sancti sunt: sicut propheta dicit: quoniam habitabo in eis (Levit. XXVI; II Cor. VI) . Tecta autem et laquearia domorum istarum cedrina et cypressina, quae incorruptibilia et odorifera dignoscuntur, directionem Dei et proximi, quae per Spiritum sanctum desuper concessa est (id est ut sancti in se sint) demonstrat.
chunks.english: “The roofs of our houses.” These houses in which Christ dwells are the saints, as the prophet says, in Leviticus, chapter twenty-six, and as Paul repeats in his second letter to the Corinthians, chapter six: “I will dwell in them.” The roofs and ceilings of these houses are made of cedar and cypress, woods known to be incorruptible and fragrant. They represent the love of God and of neighbor, granted from above through the Holy Spirit—that is, so that the saints may be holy within themselves.
chunks.notes: The printed text reads “directionem Dei et proximi”; the translation renders the evident sense “dilectionem” (the love of God and of neighbor) and records the printed reading here.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Christ the Lily and the Beloved’s Coming
chunks.latin: CAP. II.
chunks.english: Chapter 2: Christ the Lily and the Beloved’s Coming

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 25. Ego flos campi, et lilium convallium.
Ego decus mundi, ex virginitate humilium.
chunks.english: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” That is: I am the beauty of the world, born from the virgin purity of the humble.
chunks.notes: The line paraphrases Song of Songs, chapter two, verse one.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 26. Sicut lilium inter spinas. Expulso homini
de Paradiso dicitur: Maledicta terra in operibus tuis,
spinas et tribulos germinabit tibi (Gen. III) ; quae terra,
utique caro humana intelligitur, quae aculeos libidinum
et concupiscentiarum spinas producere consuevit.
Quapropter quod ait: Sicut lilium in medio
[Col. 0969B] spinarum, sic amica mea inter filias: filias haereses
dicit, quae per baptismum quasi renatae, filiarum
nomine nuncupantur; sed spinis comparatae, corrumpentes
et corruptibiles perdocentur. Quam corruptionem
Ecclesia nescit, quae liliorum sinceritati
comparata, ultro citroque redolet ac resplendet.
chunks.english:
“Like a lily among thorns.” When the human being was driven out of Paradise, Scripture says in the book of Genesis, chapter three: “Cursed is the earth because of your works; it will bring forth thorns and thistles for you.” By that earth we should understand human flesh, which is accustomed to produce the sharp points of lust and the thorns of disordered desires.

So when the text says, “Like a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among the daughters,” by “daughters” he means heresies. Because they have in a sense been reborn through baptism, they are called by the name of daughters. Yet, since they are compared to thorns, they are shown to be corrupting and corruptible. The Church knows nothing of that corruption. Compared to the purity of lilies, she gives off fragrance and shines on every side.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 27. Sicut malum inter ligna silvarum. Dicit
Psalmographus, quoniam quis in nubibus aequabitur
Domino, aut quis similis erit Deo inter filios Dei (Psal.
LXXXVIII) ? Illic adoptione, hic natura est filius; et
ideo nullus in sanctis, vel in universo genere hominum,
quamlibet filii vocabulo censeatur, Christo
similis reperitur; qui fructus sui dulcedine refectioneque
electos incomparabili decore praecedit.
chunks.english: “Like an apple tree among the trees of the forest.” The psalmist says in the Book of Psalms, Psalm eighty-eight: “Who in the clouds can be compared to the Lord? Or who is like God among the sons of God?” In that passage, the others are sons by adoption; here, Christ is Son by nature. Therefore no one among the saints, and no one in the whole human race, however much he may be called by the name of son, is found to be like Christ. Christ surpasses the elect with incomparable beauty, because of the sweetness and nourishment of his fruit.
chunks.notes: The numbering follows the Latin Psalter tradition, where Psalm eighty-eight corresponds to Psalm eighty-nine in many modern English Bibles.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 28. Sub umbra illius quem desideraveram.
[Col. 0969C] Eodem protegente quem semper adesse quaesivi, humilis
ac secura permansi.
chunks.english: “Under the shadow of the one I had desired.” Protected by the very one whose presence I had always sought, I remained humble and secure.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 29. Et fructus ejus dulcis gutturi meo. Dicit
in Evangelio Dominus: Ego sum vitis, vos estis palmites;
qui manet in me, et ego in eo, hic affert fructum
multum, quia sine me nihil potestis facere (Joan. XV) .
Quamvis igitur fructus oriatur in palmite, ad vitem
tamen deputandus est, ex cujus radice palmes cum
fructu processit; et ideo quidquid justi in bonis operibus
fructificant, totum est referendum ad Christum.
In cujus fructibus incomparabilis dulcedo sentitur.
Illi etiam sancti qui per gutturis speciem ruminare
quae gustaverant, id est meditari quae Christi sunt,
consueverant, ipsi etiam nimiam dulcedinem ex
ejus fructu percipiunt.
chunks.english:
“And his fruit was sweet to my throat.” In the Gospel of John, chapter fifteen, the Lord says: “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.”

So even though fruit appears on the branch, it must still be credited to the vine, because the branch and its fruit come from the vine’s root. In the same way, whatever fruit the righteous produce in good works must be referred entirely to Christ. In his fruits there is incomparable sweetness. And those saints who, under the image of the throat, are accustomed to chew over what they have tasted—that is, to meditate on the things of Christ—also receive a very great sweetness from his fruit.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
[Col. 0969D] Num. 30. Introduxit me in cellam vinariam. Ascensurus
in coelos Dominus praecipit apostolis ab Hierosolymis
ne discederent, dicens ad eos: Gaudete,
quia vici mundum, et vado ad Patrem; vos vero sedete
in civitate quoadusque induamini virtute ex alto. Et
sicut in Actibus apostolorum scriptum est: Tunc reversi
sunt in Jerusalem a monte qui vocatur Oliveti,
qui est juxta Jerusalem, sabbati habens iter. Et cum
intrassent in coenaculum, ascenderunt ubi manebant
Petrus et Joannes. Et post pauca, Hi erant omnes
unanimiter congregati cum mulieribus, et matre Jesu
Maria, et fratribus ejus; erat autem turba hominum
fere centum viginti (Act. I, II) in hoc loco constituti;
et superveniente Spiritu sancto repleti sunt; et cum
[Col. 0970A] coepissent loqui variis linguis, musto pleni a populo
putabantur. Tunc itaque Ecclesia in cellam vinariam
introducitur, quando haec apostolica congregatio in
unitate permanens, Spiritu sancto repletur, sicut et
Apostolus dicit: In uno Spiritu omnes nos baptizati
sumus, sive servi, sive liberi, et omnes in uno Spiritu
potati sumus (I Cor. XII) . Quia vero charitas per Spiritum
sanctum piorum in corde diffunditur, statim
subjunxit, Ordinavit in me charitatem. Haec enim est
ordinata charitas, ut diligat homo proximum suum
tanquam seipsum; sic vero diligat Deum, ut etiam
seipsum abneget propter ipsum. Diligitur autem in
malis quoque non iniquitas quam ipsi faciunt, sed
creatura in qua boni a Deo formati sunt. Sed et illa
ordinata charitas, ut servi Dominum non sicut malefactores
[Col. 0970B] sentiant, nec sicut lascivientes exsecrabili
amore se diligant, sed etiam ubi necesse fuerit semetipsos
mutuo expulsa superstitione cum libertate
corripiant, secundum illud: Meliora sunt vulnera diligentis,
quam fraudulenta oscula blandientis (Prov.
XXVII) ; et iterum: Qui arguunt laudabuntur, et super
ipsos veniet benedictio (Prov. XXIV) .
chunks.english:
“He brought me into the wine cellar.” When the Lord was about to ascend into heaven, he commanded the apostles not to leave Jerusalem. He said to them, “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world and I am going to the Father. But you, remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.”

And, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, chapters one and two: “Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. And when they had entered the upper room, they went up to where Peter and John were staying.” A little later it says: “All these were gathered together with one mind, with the women, and with Mary the mother of Jesus, and with his brothers.” And the crowd of people in that place was about one hundred twenty. When the Holy Spirit came upon them, they were filled; and when they began to speak in different languages, the people thought they were full of new wine.

So the Church is brought into the wine cellar when this apostolic gathering, remaining in unity, is filled with the Holy Spirit. As the Apostle also says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter twelve: “In one Spirit we were all baptized, whether slaves or free, and we were all made to drink of one Spirit.”

Because love is poured into the hearts of the faithful through the Holy Spirit, the text immediately adds: “He ordered love in me.” This is ordered love: that a person loves his neighbor as himself, but loves God in such a way that he even denies himself for God’s sake. Even in wicked people, what is loved is not the wrongdoing they commit, but the creature in them, because they were made good by God.

This too is ordered love: that servants should not experience the Lord as if they were criminals, nor love one another with a shameful, indulgent kind of love. Instead, when necessary, they should freely correct one another, after superstition has been cast out. As Scripture says in the Book of Proverbs, chapter twenty-seven: “The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who flatters.” And again, in the Book of Proverbs, chapter twenty-four: “Those who give correction will be praised, and blessing will come upon them.”
chunks.notes: The opening speech combines themes from the farewell discourse and the command to wait in Jerusalem before Pentecost.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 31. Fulcite me floribus, stipate me malis.
Sanctorum coetibus conjungi vel circumdari desiderat,
quae pio et casto amore languescit; quia languor
non est morbi, sed ineffabilis desiderii secundum
illud: Defecit in salutari tuo anima mea, et in
verbum tuum supersperavi, defecerunt oculi mei in
eloquium tuum dicentes: Quando consolaberis me
(Psal. CXVIII) ? Felices illi qui tali profectu proficiunt:
[Col. 0970C] quodammodo enim, qui multum desiderat, languescit
et deficit donec optata vel quaesita reperiat.
chunks.english:
“Support me with flowers; surround me with apples.” She longs to be joined to, and surrounded by, the assemblies of the saints, because she is faint with a holy and chaste love. This faintness is not the weakness of sickness, but the weakness of an inexpressible desire. As it says in the Book of Psalms, Psalm one hundred eighteen: “My soul has fainted for your salvation, and I have hoped beyond hope in your word. My eyes have failed as they look for your promise, saying, ‘When will you comfort me?’”

Blessed are those who advance by such progress. For, in a certain sense, the person who longs intensely grows faint and fails until he finds what he hopes for and seeks.
chunks.notes: The numbering follows the Latin Psalter tradition, where Psalm one hundred eighteen corresponds to Psalm one hundred nineteen in many modern English Bibles.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 32. Laeva ejus sub capite meo. Ipse Salomon
in Proverbiis ait: Beatus homo qui invenit sapientiam,
et affluit prudentia; longitudo dierum in dextra ejus
et in sinistra ejus divitiae et gloria. Ac sic electa Christi
Ecclesia sinistram habens sub capite, temporalia
sibi subjecta describit; et dextra ejus se amplexari,
dum aeterna concupiscit, edocuit.
chunks.english:
“His left hand is under my head.” Solomon himself says in the Book of Proverbs: “Blessed is the person who finds wisdom and overflows with prudence. Length of days is in her right hand, and in her left hand are riches and glory.”

So the chosen Church of Christ, by having his left hand under her head, shows that temporal things are placed beneath her. And by saying that his right hand embraces her, she teaches that she desires eternal things.
chunks.notes: The quotation echoes Proverbs, chapter three, verses thirteen through sixteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 33. Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem, per capreas.
Filias Jerusalem, sanctas et pacificas doctorum animas
dicit; quas, per munda et velocia animalia quae
ruminare non desinunt, et in campis sanctarum
Scripturarum aluntur, conjurat, ne suscitare faciant,
donec ipsa velit: quod Paulum apostolum fecisse
[Col. 0970D] cognoscimus, cum virginibus de conservanda sanctimonia,
non praeceptum, sed consilium dedit (I Cor.
VII) ; et in Evangelio diviti dicitur: Si vis perfectus
essse, vade et vende omnia quae habes, et da pauperibus
(Matth. XIX) . Et alio loco ubi spadones laudantur, qui
se ipsos castraverunt propter regnum coelorum; et statim
adjicitur, qui potest capere capiat. Et iterum Apostolus,
cum ad continentiam hortatur: Hoc ad utilitatem
vestram dico (inquit), non ut laqueum vobis injiciam,
sed ad id quod honestum est, hortor, et quod facultatem
praebeat sine impedimento Deum obsecrandi
(I Cor. VII) . Et rursus ad Philemonem: Sine consilio
autem tuo nihil volui facere, uti ne velut ex necessitate
bonum tuum esset, sed voluntarium. Tunc enim dilecta
[Col. 0971A] quoadusque velit nullo modo suscitatur,
quando sanctorum vota voluntate spontanea Domino
offeruntur.
chunks.english:
“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles.” By “daughters of Jerusalem” he means the holy and peaceful souls of teachers. He adjures them by clean and swift animals, which never stop chewing the cud and which feed in the fields of the holy Scriptures, not to make the beloved awaken until she herself wishes.

We know that the apostle Paul acted in this way when, regarding virgins preserving holiness, he gave not a command but counsel, as in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter seven. And in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter nineteen, the rich man is told: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, and give to the poor.” In another place, those eunuchs are praised who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven, and immediately it is added: “Let the one who can accept this accept it.”

Again, when the Apostle urges continence, he says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter seven: “I say this for your benefit, not to throw a noose around you, but to encourage what is honorable, and what gives freedom to pray to God without hindrance.” And again, in Paul’s letter to Philemon: “I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your good deed would not be as if forced by necessity, but voluntary.”

So the beloved is in no way awakened until she wishes, when the vows of the saints are offered to the Lord by their own free will.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 34. Vox dilecti mei. Haec vox Christi, quae
in hac prophetia tantum commemoratur, non inscite
de illa accipitur qua genus mortuorum hominum in
Evangelio suscitantur, sicut ipse pronuntiat dicens:
Amen amen dico vobis, quia veniet hora in qua omnes
qui in monumentis sunt audient vocem ejus, et procedent
qui bona fecerunt in resurrectionem vitae (Joan. V) .
Et in Apocalypsi dicitur: Beatus qui habitat partem in
resurrectione prima (Apoc. XX) . Ille in prima resurrectione
partem invenit, qui erutus de mala consuetudine,
tanquam a morte Christo vivificante resurgit.
chunks.english:
“The voice of my beloved.” This voice of Christ, which is only mentioned in this prophecy, may rightly be understood as the voice by which, in the Gospel, the race of dead humanity is raised. Christ himself declares in the Gospel of John, chapter five: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life.”

And in the Book of Revelation, chapter twenty, it says: “Blessed is the one who has a share in the first resurrection.” A person has a share in the first resurrection when he is rescued from an evil habit and, as if from death, rises again because Christ gives him life.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 35. Ecce iste venit saliens in montibus. Venit
[Col. 0971B] Christus saliens in montibus, cum perfectior perfectis
apparuit; transiliens colles, cum omnem sanctorum
altitudinem suae majestatis excellentia superavit.
chunks.english: “Look, here he comes, leaping over the mountains.” Christ comes leaping over the mountains when he appears, more perfect than the perfect. He comes bounding over the hills when, by the excellence of his majesty, he surpasses every height of the saints.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 36. Similis est dilectus meus capreae. Similis
est capreae, quia in similitudine carnis peccati (Rom.
VIII) , nobis apparuit; similis etiam cervorum hinnulo,
quia de sanctis qui serpentem vicerunt, secundum
carnem duxit originem.
chunks.english: “My beloved is like a gazelle.” He is like a gazelle because, as Paul says in his letter to the Romans, chapter eight, he appeared to us “in the likeness of sinful flesh.” He is also like a young stag, because according to the flesh he took his origin from the saints who conquered the serpent.
chunks.notes: “The saints who conquered the serpent” refers to Christ’s righteous ancestors and, ultimately, the victory over the devil figured as the serpent.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 37. En ipse stat post parietem. Stat post
parietem nostrum cum induitur velamine corporis
nostri.
chunks.english: “See, he stands behind our wall.” He stands behind our wall when he is clothed with the covering of our body.
chunks.notes: The “wall” is interpreted as Christ’s assumed human flesh.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 38. Respiciens per fenestras. Cum quiddam
sui occuluit, quiddam autem manifestavit; quasi per
fenestras et cancellos prospexit. Non enim se ex toto
praecipue secundum Deum ostendit, qui Patrem videre
[Col. 0971C] cupienti Philippo dixit: Tanto tempore vobiscum
sum, et non cognovistis me; et alio loco: Qui diligit
me mandata mea custodit et ego diligam eum et manifestabo
ei meipsum (Joan. XIV) . Vel tunc per fenestras
et cancellos prospexit, quando plebem in parabolis
edocuit. Potest etiam intelligi quod tunc per fenestras
prospexit, quando in passione, lancea perforato latere,
sanguine et aqua manante, redemptionis et lavacri
sacramenta produxit.
chunks.english:
“Looking through the windows.” Since he concealed something of himself and revealed something, he looked out, as it were, through windows and latticework. He did not show himself completely, especially according to his divinity. This is why he said to Philip, who wanted to see the Father, in the Gospel of John, chapter fourteen: “Have I been with you so long, and you have not known me?” And in another place in the same chapter: “The one who loves me keeps my commandments, and I will love him and reveal myself to him.”

Or we may say that he looked through the windows and latticework when he taught the people in parables. It can also be understood that he looked through the windows at the time of his Passion, when his side was pierced by the lance and blood and water flowed out, bringing forth the sacraments of redemption and washing.
chunks.notes: “Washing” refers to baptism; the blood and water from Christ’s side are read sacramentally.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 39. Dilectus meus loquitur mihi. Dilectus in
hoc libro saepe describitur: quis enim tam dilectus
Ecclesiae quam ille propter quem martyres animas
posuerunt? Surge, propera et veni: surge, crede; propera,
peracto cursu pii laboris praemium suscipe.
Amica mea, reconciliata mihi per mortem; formosa
[Col. 0971D] mea, munda facta per lavacrum.
chunks.english:
“My beloved speaks to me.” The beloved is described often in this book. For who is so beloved to the Church as the one for whom the martyrs laid down their lives?

“Rise, hurry, and come.” Rise—that is, believe. Hurry—that is, after completing the course of devoted labor, receive the reward. “My beloved,” because you have been reconciled to me through death. “My beautiful one,” because you have been made clean through the washing of baptism.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 40. Jam enim hiems transiit. Quia temporalis
tribulatio finem accepit.
chunks.english: “For now the winter has passed.” That is, temporary tribulation has come to an end.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 41. Imber abiit et recessit. Crebra et multiplex
tentatio, vel paganorum persecutio quievit.
chunks.english: “The rain is gone and has withdrawn.” That is, frequent and many-sided temptation, or the persecution by pagans, has ceased.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 42. Flores apparuerunt in terra. Sancti redundaverunt
in mundo, mense Novorum, quando
Pascha celebratur, exorti; quibus Apostolus dicit:
Si consurrexistis cum Christo, quae sursum sunt sapite,
non quae super terram (Col. III) .
chunks.english: “Flowers have appeared on the earth.” The saints have abounded in the world, springing up in the month of new things, when Easter is celebrated. To them the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Colossians, chapter three: “If you have risen with Christ, set your mind on the things above, not on the things that are on the earth.”
chunks.notes: “The month of new things” refers to the springtime and Easter season, when new life appears.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 43. Tempus putationis advenit. Hi qui in domo
Domini sunt plantati, adhibita disciplinae falce,
ab omni superstitione purgati, venturis fructibus praeparantur.
chunks.english: “The time of pruning has arrived.” Those who are planted in the house of the Lord are purified from every superstition by the pruning hook of discipline, and so they are prepared for the fruits that are to come.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 44. Vox turturis audita est in terra. Anima, in Evangelio, octoginta quatuor annorum castissima vidua, non recedens de templo, in jejuniis et orationibus Christum agnoscit, et loquitur de eo omnibus qui exspectabant redemptionem Israel (Luc. II) . Istarum quoque avium combinationem in sacrificium offerri mandavit, qui nil omnino in oblatione Dei praeclarum, nisi cum fideles corpore et spiritu sanctificati Domino offeruntur.
chunks.english: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in the land.” In the Gospel, Anna, a most chaste widow eighty-four years old, never left the temple. With fasting and prayers she recognized Christ, and she spoke about him to everyone who was waiting for the redemption of Israel, as told in the Gospel of Luke, chapter two. God also commanded that a pair of these birds be offered in sacrifice, because nothing is truly excellent in an offering to God unless the faithful themselves are offered to the Lord, sanctified in body and in spirit.
chunks.notes: The Latin reads “Anima,” but the reference is clearly to Anna in the Gospel of Luke.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 45. Ficus protulit grossos suos. Tandem etiam Synagoga credentes in Christo produxit Israelitas, sicut et Apostolus ait: Nolo vos ignorare mysterium hoc, quia caecitas ex parte contigit in Israel, donec plenitudo gentium intraret, et sic omnis Israel salvus fieret (Rom. XI) .
chunks.english: “The fig tree has brought out its early fruit.” In the end, even the Synagogue brought forth Israelites who believed in Christ. As the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eleven: “I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery: a blindness has come upon part of Israel until the fullness of the nations comes in, and so all Israel will be saved.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 46. Vineae florentes et dederunt odorem. Congregationes clericorum, monachorum quoque et virginum in Ecclesia proficiunt, et per bonam famam et conversationem innotuerunt.
chunks.english: “The vineyards are in bloom and have given their fragrance.” Communities of clergy, monks, and virgins grow and flourish within the Church, and they become known through their good reputation and their holy way of life.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 47. Surge, amica mea, et speciosa mea. Piis appellationibus semper hortatur Ecclesia ut relictis temporalibus ad aeterna suspiret.
chunks.english: “Rise up, my friend, my beautiful one.” With these loving names, Christ continually urges the Church to leave behind temporal things and to long for eternal things.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 48. Columba mea in foraminibus petrae. Non aliud Ecclesia columba vocatur, nisi quia est sine dolo et Spiritu sancto repletur; habitat in foraminibus petrae, quia semper receptaculum habet in his, ex quibus sanata est, vulneribus Christi. Recipitur etiam in cavernam maceriae, cum sancta ex Scripturis consolatione fovetur, vel cum praecedentium sanctorum meritis atque orationibus ex toto protegitur. In his foraminibus petrae, Thomas apostolus tanquam columba, protectionem invenit, cum post resurrectionem contrectatis Christi vulnerum locis, remota omni dubietate, Deus meus et Dominus meus (Joan. XX) , fideliter exclamavit.
chunks.english: “My dove in the clefts of the rock.” The Church is called a dove for no other reason than that she is without deceit and is filled with the Holy Spirit. She lives in the clefts of the rock because she always finds refuge in the very wounds of Christ, the wounds by which she has been healed. She is also received into the hollow of the wall when she is warmed and strengthened by the holy consolation of the Scriptures, or when she is completely protected by the merits and prayers of the saints who have gone before her. In these clefts of the rock, the apostle Thomas found protection like a dove. After the resurrection, when he touched the places of Christ’s wounds, all doubt was removed, and he cried out in faith, as recorded in the Gospel of John, chapter twenty: “My God and my Lord.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 49. Ostende mihi faciem tuam, Sion. Sion interpretatur speculatio, quae merito in illis intelligitur qui cum Apostolo dicunt: Nos autem gloriam Dei speculantes, in eamdem imaginem transformamur a claritate in claritatem tanquam a Domini spiritu. Et iterum: Non contemplantibus nobis quae videntur, sed quae non videntur (II Cor. III) . Quae enim videntur temporalia sunt, quae autem non videntur aeterna sunt. Haec itaque invitatur ut semper ante Deum assistat, sicut Elias qui dicebat: Vivit Dominus, in cujus conspectu asto hodie (IV Reg. III) ; nec sit de illis quos propheta denotat dicens: Verterunt ad me tergum et non faciem (Jerem. II) ; et, vox tua, inquit, in auribus meis (III Reg. XVII) ; et, clamaverunt justi, et Dominus exaudivit eos et ex omnibus tribulationibus eorum liberavit eos (Psal. XXXIII) .
chunks.english: “Show me your face, Zion.” The name Zion is interpreted as “contemplation,” and rightly refers to those who say with the Apostle, in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter three: “We, contemplating the glory of God, are being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.” And again: “We look not at the things that are seen, but at the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” Zion, then, is invited always to stand before God, like Elijah, who said in the Fourth Book of Kings, chapter three: “The Lord lives, in whose sight I stand today.” She must not be among those whom the prophet rebukes in the book of Jeremiah, chapter two: “They have turned their back to me, and not their face.” And, it says, “your voice is in my ears”—cited in the printed text as the Third Book of Kings, chapter seventeen. And in Psalm thirty-three: “The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them, and delivered them from all their troubles.”
chunks.notes: The second quotation attributed here to Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter three, actually corresponds to chapter four, verse eighteen. The citation is preserved in translation as the author presents it, with the wording translated accurately. “Your voice is in my ears” is the Song of Songs (chapter two) resuming; the printed reference to the Third Book of Kings, chapter seventeen, is misplaced. The references to the books of Kings are spoken in Migne's numbering (Third and Fourth Kings = First and Second Kings in modern Bibles).

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 50. Vox enim tua dulcis. Orationes sanctorum semper Domino acceptae, gratiaque ejus praesentes, quia de Christi lumine acceperunt, ut in decore justitiae permanerent.
chunks.english: “For your voice is sweet.” The prayers of the saints are always pleasing to the Lord and always present before his grace, because they have received from the light of Christ the power to remain in the beauty of righteousness.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 51. Capite nobis vulpes parvulas. Dicit per parabolam in Evangelio Dominus (Matth. XIII) cum crevisset herba, et fructum fecisset, tunc apparuerunt zizania: id est, proficiente Ecclesia numerosae etiam haereses surrexerunt, vel in illa fide permanente quam prave sentirent investigatae sunt.
