Sic et ille Samson, qui interpretatur sol, captis trecentis vulpibus, eorum caudis ignem apposuit, et fructus inimicorum accendit (Judic. XV) . Semper enim haeretici in primordiis, velut ficta religione conspicui, in extremis suis ignem trahunt, gehennae incendio deputati. Et ideo Capite nobis vulpes: convincite haereticos, eorumque versutias sanctarum Scripturarum concludite testimoniis. Quos vulpes parvulas dicit, quia nihil magni secundum rectam fidem intelligendo continent; omne enim quod sapiunt, exhibent; qui pusilli sunt demoliuntur vineas, subvertunt plebes, pravis eas traditionibus corrumpentes. Vinea nostra floruit. Ecclesia catholica indeclinabili augmento proficit.
chunks.english: “Catch the little foxes for us.” In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter thirteen, the Lord says in a parable that when the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds appeared. In other words, as the Church advanced, many heresies also arose; or else, while that faith endured, the heresies were found out in what they wrongly believed. So too Samson, whose name is interpreted as “sun,” caught three hundred foxes, set fire to their tails, and burned the crops of his enemies, as told in the book of Judges, chapter fifteen. Heretics always appear impressive at the beginning, as though distinguished by a religion that is only feigned; but at their end they drag fire behind them, being destined for the fire of Gehenna. Therefore, “Catch the foxes for us” means: refute the heretics, and trap their tricks with the testimonies of the holy Scriptures. He calls them “little foxes” because, according to the rule of right faith, there is nothing great in their understanding. Whatever wisdom they claim, they put it all on display. Though they are small, they destroy the vineyards; they overthrow peoples by corrupting them with evil traditions. “Our vineyard has flourished”: the Catholic Church advances with growth that cannot be turned aside.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 52. Dilectus meus mihi, et ego illi. Dicit Apostolus: Erunt duo in carne una. Sacramentum hoc magnum est, ego autem dico in Christo et Ecclesia (Ephes. V) . De ipso enim eadem Ecclesia dicit: Dominus pars haereditatis meae (Psalm. XV) . Et iterum a Patre Filio dicitur: Postula a me, et dabo tibi gentes haereditatem tuam, et possessionem tuam terminos terrae (Psalm. II) . Habet igitur Christus Ecclesiam in suo corpore et Ecclesia Christum in capite: quae connexio quia dissociari non potest, merito dixit: Dilectus meus mihi.
chunks.english: “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” The Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter five: “The two will be one flesh. This is a great mystery; but I am speaking of Christ and the Church.” Speaking of Christ, the same Church says in Psalm fifteen: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance.” And again, the Father says to the Son in Psalm two: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.” Therefore Christ has the Church in his body, and the Church has Christ as her head. Because this bond cannot be broken apart, she rightly says: “My beloved is mine.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 53. Qui pascitur inter lilia. Pascitur inter lilia Christus quando corpus ejus, quod est Ecclesia, sanctorum et virginum coetibus decoratur
chunks.english: “He pastures among the lilies.” Christ is said to pasture among the lilies when his body, which is the Church, is adorned with communities of saints and virgins.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 54. Donec exspiret dies, et inclinentur umbrae. Donec evangelica traditio in clariore luce proficiat, et figurae Veteris Testamenti, quae velut umbrae, in ritu sacrificiorum, typicis observationibus praecesserunt, depellantur.
chunks.english: “Until the day breathes and the shadows turn away.” This means: until the gospel tradition advances in a clearer light, and the figures of the Old Testament—which had gone before like shadows in the ritual of sacrifices and in symbolic observances—are driven away.
chunks.notes: The printed lemma reads “exspiret” where the Vulgate has “aspiret”; the exposition (the day advancing into clearer light) requires the sense of the day’s breathing forth, which the translation keeps.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 55. Revertere, similis esto, dilecte mihi. Dum dilectum insinuat regredi, similemque capreae et hinnulo dicit, Christi in coelos ascensionem, mundis et velocibus animalibus comparandam demonstrat. Haec enim celeri saltu, montium altiora transiliunt; supergressus est autem Christus omnia quae videntur excelsa, quia de ipso Apostolus dicit: Propter quod Deus exaltavit illum, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen, ut in nomine Jesu omne genu flectatur, coelestium, terrestrium et infernorum, et omnis lingua confiteatur quia Dominus Jesus in gloria est Dei Patris (Philip II) . Bethel autem interpretatur domus Dei: ergo super montes Bethel, quia omnibus sanctis qui in coelo et in terra sunt, Christum praedicat potentiorem
chunks.english: “Return, my beloved; be like a gazelle or a young stag.” When the text suggests that the beloved goes back, and when it compares him to a gazelle and a young stag, it shows that Christ’s ascension into heaven is being compared to clean and swift animals. These animals leap quickly over the higher places of the mountains. Christ, however, has surpassed everything that appears exalted, because the Apostle says of him in Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two: “Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of God the Father.” Now Bethel means “house of God.” So the phrase “upon the mountains of Bethel” proclaims that Christ is more powerful than all the saints who are in heaven and on earth.
chunks.notes: The Latin text ends this chunk mid-sentence or without a final period; the translation closes the thought as far as the transmitted text allows.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: The Bride Searches for Christ and Beholds His Church
chunks.latin: CAP. III.
chunks.english: Chapter 3: The Bride Searches for Christ and Beholds His Church

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 56. In lectulo per noctes quaesivi. In his qui in fide dormitant, et ignorantiae tenebris deleti sunt, quaesivit Christum, quem diligit Ecclesia; sed vide quid sequitur: Quaesivi illum, et non inveni. Dicit Dominus ad Adam: In sudore vultus tui comedes panem tuum (Gen. III) . Non enim qui vitio quodam vel sopore inertiae resolvuntur, ad illius panis qui de coelo descendit, esum, cito perveniunt, sed qui sanctis laboribus invigilaverint, ipsi eum reperiunt.
chunks.english: “On my bed, through the nights, I sought him.” Among those who sleep in the faith, and who are blotted out by the darkness of ignorance, the Church sought Christ, the one she loves. But notice what follows: “I sought him and did not find him.” The Lord says to Adam in Genesis, chapter three: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” For those who collapse through some vice, or through the drowsiness of laziness, do not quickly come to eat that bread which came down from heaven. Rather, the people who keep watch through holy labor are the ones who find him.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 57. Surgam et circuibo civitatem. Consideravi omnem gloriam praesentis saeculi, inspexi congregationes infidelium et diversas sectas philosophorum; sed nec illic reperi quem diligit anima mea.
chunks.english: “I will rise and go around the city.” I considered all the glory of the present age. I looked into the gatherings of unbelievers and the various schools of the philosophers. But even there I did not find the one whom my soul loves.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 58. Invenerunt me vigiles. Disputaverunt contra me saeculi sapientes idolorumque cultores, multa inaniter perscrutantes, pluresque libros irritis laboribus conficientes, quibus dixi: Cur incassum superfluo conatu vexamini? Cur frustra vehementer ingenia vestra atteritis? num quem diligit anima mea vidistis? Quandoquidem falso nomine sapientiae gloriamini, stultam fecit Deus sapientiam (I Cor. II) vestram, quia Christum illic invenire minime valuistis.
chunks.english: “The watchmen found me.” The wise people of this world and the worshipers of idols argued against me. They investigated many things in vain and produced many books with fruitless labor. To them I said: Why are you exhausting yourselves in useless effort? Why are you wearing out your minds so fiercely, and for nothing? Have you seen the one whom my soul loves? Since you boast under the false name of wisdom, God has made your wisdom foolish, as Paul says in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter two. For you were not able to find Christ there.
chunks.notes: The printed Latin cites First Corinthians, chapter two, but the phrase “God has made wisdom foolish” corresponds most closely to First Corinthians, chapter one.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 59. Paululum cum pertransissem. Cum pertransissem hujusmodi homines qui in saeculo vana scientia clari putantur, et cum eorum superstitiosis adinventionibus restitissem, eorumque sapientiam stultam judicassem, invenit quem diligit anima mea. Inde est quod Apostolus de talibus dicit: Sapientiam loquimur inter perfectos, sapientiam autem non hujus saeculi, sed loquimur Dei sapientiam in mysterio, quae abscondita est, quam praedestinavit Deus ante saecula in gloriam nostram (I Cor. I) : et quia ipsa sapientia quae Christus est, apud tales non reperitur, sequitur: quam nemo principum hujus saeculi cognovit; si enim cognovissent, nunquam Dominum gloriae crucifixissent: sicut scriptum est, quod oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis ascendit, quae praeparavit Deus his qui diligunt illum (Ibid.) . Sed quia apud spirituales invenit illum quem diligit sponsa, audi quid sequatur: Nobis autem revelavit Deus per Spiritum suum; Spiritus autem omnia scrutatur, etiam profunda Dei (Ibid.) .
chunks.english: “When I had passed on a little way.” When I had passed beyond people of this sort—people who are considered famous in the world because of empty learning—and when I had resisted their superstitious inventions and judged their wisdom to be foolish, then my soul found the one she loves. That is why the Apostle says about such things in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter one: “We speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age. Rather, we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predestined before the ages for our glory.” And because that wisdom itself, which is Christ, is not found among such people, Paul continues: “None of the rulers of this age knew it. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.” And again: “As it is written: What no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart—these are the things God has prepared for those who love him.” But because the bride finds the one she loves among spiritual people, listen to what follows: “God has revealed it to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.”
chunks.notes: The printed Latin cites First Corinthians, chapter one, but the passage quoted is from First Corinthians, chapter two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 60. Tenui eum, nec dimittam. Ita namque adhaerebo Christo, in ejus fide perseverabo, donec ipsum in Synagogae populis tanquam in domo matris praedicans, introducam in cubiculum genitricis meae: ut Judaei, qui eum hactenus negabant ore, corde recipiant; illuminatisque mentis oculis eorum, in cubiculum, in secreto sanctarum Scripturarum consistentem, qui nobis olim revelatus est aliquando reperiant. Vel tunc Christus in domo matris inducitur, cum ad Jerusalem coelestem Christianus populus, qui est corpus ipsius, sociatur. Ubi est quod oculus non vidit, nec auris audivit, nec in cor hominis, etc.
chunks.english: “I held him, and I will not let him go.” In this way I will cling to Christ and persevere in faith in him, until, by preaching him among the people of the synagogue, as in the house of my mother, I bring him into the chamber of the one who bore me. Then the Jews, who until now have denied him with their mouths, may receive him in their hearts. And when the eyes of their minds have been enlightened, they may at last find him in that inner chamber: that is, in the hidden meaning of the holy Scriptures, where he has stood all along, though he was revealed to us earlier. Or else Christ is brought into the house of his mother when the Christian people, who are his body, are joined to the heavenly Jerusalem. There is the reality of which Scripture says: “What no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and what has not entered the human heart,” and so on.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 61. Adjuro vos filias Jerusalem. Hanc sententiam jam in superioribus constituit, et in quantum Deus audivit, adhibitis testimoniis nos pertractasse meminimus. Sed idcirco iterum in hoc libro arbitror repetitum, ne quisquam doctorum vel muneribus sollicitet, vel minis deterreat credituros, sed tantum quae sancta sunt praedicet, et voluntarie ad fidem vel religionem credituros sive convertendos adducat.
chunks.english: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” He has already set down this saying earlier, and, as God heard us, we remember that we examined it then with supporting testimonies. But I think it is repeated again in this book for this reason: no teacher should entice future believers with gifts or frighten them with threats. Instead, he should simply preach what is holy and bring people to faith and religion willingly, whether they are already coming to believe or are being converted.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 62. Quae est ista quae ascendit per desertum. Per desertum ascendit Ecclesia, quando populus gentium, fide occupans credentium multitudinem, proficit. De ipsa enim in Psalmis canitur: Posuit desertum in stagna aquarum, et terram sine aqua in exitus uquarum (Psalm. CVI et CXIII) . Virgulta fumi ex aromatibus, orationes dicit quae ex cordis compunctione ad Dominum ascendunt a sanctis. Solet enim fumus lacrymas excitare. Myrrha et thus, et universi pulveris pigmenta, mortificationis insignia, vel diversa gratiarum quae in electis redundant dona, insinuant.
chunks.english: “Who is this who comes up through the desert?” The Church comes up through the desert when the people of the nations advance in faith and fill up the multitude of believers. For of the Church it is sung in the Psalms, in psalm one hundred six and psalm one hundred thirteen: “He turned the desert into pools of water, and the waterless land into springs of water.” The “little columns of smoke from spices” mean the prayers that rise up to the Lord from the saints, prayers born from a pierced and repentant heart. Smoke, after all, often brings tears to the eyes. Myrrh, frankincense, and every powdered perfume point to the signs of mortification, or to the different gifts of grace that overflow among the chosen.
chunks.notes: The Latin has “uquarum,” evidently a scribal or typographical error for “aquarum.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 63. An lectulum Salomonis. Lectulus Salomonis, requies Christi est; quae requies Ecclesiae convenienter accipitur, quam sub numero in Psalmis legimus electam: Quoniam, inquit, elegit Dominus Sion, elegit eam in habitationem sibi. Haec requies mea in saeculum saeculi, hic habitabo, quoniam elegi cam (Psal. LXXV) . In sexagenario autem numero, quia sexagenarius totus suis partibus constat, et per denarium ascendit, merito ex fortissimis Israel deseribuntur, qui praesente Domino in Ecclesiae custodiam deputantur. Ad ipsam etiam dicitur per prophetam: Super muros tuos, Jerusalem, custodes constitui; tota die et nocte perpetuo non tacebunt. Omnes tenentes gladios, ad bella doctissimi. Et uniuscujusque ensis super femur suum (Isai. LXII) . Ipsis enim Apostolus dicit: State ergo succincti lumbos vestros in veritate, et induite loricam justitiae, et calceati pedes in praeparationem Evangelii pacis, in omnibus sumentes scutum fidei in quo possitis omnia tela nequissimi ignea exstinguere; et galeam salutis assumite, et gladium spiritus quod est verbum Dei (Ephes. VI) . Illi itaque sunt ad bella doctissimi, qui contra carnis suae concupiscentias noverunt repugnare; et ille ensem super femur suum utiliter bajulat, qui carnales fluxus atque libidines spiritali cibo mortificat. Quicunque igitur hujusmodi in Ecclesia reperiuntur, hi fortes ex fortissimis Israel, contemplando Deum, esse noscuntur.
chunks.english: “Look at Solomon’s bed.” Solomon’s bed is the resting place of Christ. This resting place is rightly understood as the Church, which we read was chosen, according to its number, in the Psalms, in Psalm seventy-five: “The Lord has chosen Zion; he has chosen her as a dwelling for himself. This is my resting place forever and ever; here I will dwell, because I have chosen her.” Now the number sixty is fitting here, because sixty is complete in all its parts and rises by way of the number ten. So it is fitting that the strongest men of Israel are described as those who, while the Lord is present, are appointed to guard the Church. To the Church herself the prophet says, in Isaiah, chapter sixty-two: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they will never keep silent.” These are “all holding swords, most skilled in battle,” and “each one’s sword is upon his thigh.” For to these people the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter six: “Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth. Put on the breastplate of righteousness. Let your feet be shod with readiness for the Gospel of peace. In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. Take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.” Therefore, those are the people most skilled in battle who know how to fight against the desires of their own flesh. And the person usefully carries a sword upon his thigh who puts to death bodily impulses and lusts by spiritual nourishment. So whoever is found in the Church living in this way is known to be one of the strong, from the strongest of Israel, because he contemplates God.
chunks.notes: The Psalm citation in the printed Latin is uncertain: the quoted words correspond to Psalm one hundred thirty-one in the Vulgate numbering, not to Psalm seventy-five as printed. The Latin “An lectulum” is likely a corrupt reading for “En lectulum,” “Look at the bed.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 64. Ferculum fecit sibi rex Salomon. Ubi ciborum exhibitio scribitur, fides illic credentium per quam Christus advertitur. Nam cum Dominus mulieri Samaritanae ad puteum loqueretur, et illa regrediens majestatem ejus caeteris in civitate commanentibus nuntiasset, discipuli ejus supervenientes rogabant eum dicentes: Rabbi, manduca. Ille autem dixit eis: Ego cibum habeo manducare quem vos nescitis. Et paulo post: ex civitate illa multi crediderunt in eum Samaritanorum (Joan. IV) . Horum fidem, cibum sibi futurum ostendit, quando discipulis hoc se comesturum quod illi nescirent, paulo ante praedixit. Sed in hoc loco, ut sequentia docent, nomen ferculi, magis instrumentum in quo aliquid deferatur, vel, sicut alia editio habet, gestatorium, quam ipsum cibum ostendit. De lignis Libani: de praecipuis in Ecclesia sanctis.
chunks.english: “King Solomon made himself a carrying couch.” Where a serving of food is described, we may understand the faith of believers, by which Christ is perceived. For when the Lord was speaking with the Samaritan woman at the well, and she went back and announced his majesty to the others who lived in the city, his disciples arrived and urged him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.” But he said to them, in the Gospel of John, chapter four: “I have food to eat that you do not know about.” And a little later the Gospel says: “Many Samaritans from that city believed in him.” He showed that their faith would become food for him, when shortly before he had told the disciples that he would eat something they did not know about. But in this passage, as the words that follow make clear, the term “carrying couch” refers not so much to the food itself as to the object in which something is carried—or, as another edition has it, a portable litter. “From the wood of Lebanon” means: from the most excellent saints in the Church.
chunks.notes: The Latin word “ferculum” can mean a dish or course of food, but in the Song of Songs it refers to a portable couch or litter; Justus explicitly explains the double sense.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 65. Columnas ejus fecit argenteas. Sustentacula Ecclesiae praeparavit ex doctis vel apostolis suis, sicut Paulus vas electionis ad Galatas scripsit: Cum cognovissent, inquit, gratiam Dei Jacobus, Cephas, et Joannes, qui videbantur columnae esse, dextras mihi et Barnabae dederunt societatis (Gal. II) .
chunks.english: “He made its columns of silver.” Christ prepared the supports of the Church from his learned teachers and apostles. As Paul, the chosen vessel, wrote in his letter to the Galatians, chapter two: “When James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, recognized the grace of God, they gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 66: Reclinatorium aureum. In illis bene epulaturus Christus reclinatorium invenit, qui intellectu sincero praediti, velut aurum in sancta congregatione refulgent.
chunks.english: “Its reclining place was gold.” Christ finds a place to recline, and to feast well, in those who are gifted with sincere understanding and shine like gold in the holy congregation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 67. Ascensum purpureum. Ascensus purpureus, martyrum eximiam perfectionem in effusione sanguinis docet.
chunks.english: “Its ascent was purple.” The purple ascent teaches us about the outstanding perfection of the martyrs in the shedding of their blood.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 68. Media charitate construit. Ut ista omnia Ecclesiae ornamenta construeret, nulla alia causa est nisi quia dilexit nos et tradidit semetipsum pro nobis oblationem et hostiam Deo in odorem suavitatis (Ephes. V) .
chunks.english: “Its middle was built with love.” There is no other reason why Christ built all these adornments of the Church except this: he loved us and handed himself over for us, as Paul says in his letter to the Ephesians, chapter five, “an offering and sacrifice to God, a sweet-smelling fragrance.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 69. Egredimini et videte, filiae Sion. Semper prae oculis habete, sanctae animae, regem Salomonem, pacificum nostrum, qui Christus est, quemadmodum passionem sustinuit (Marc., XV; Joan. XIX) , ut genus humanum ab interitu liberaret; inspicite eum in diademate quo coronavit eum mater sua: in illa spinea corona quam capiti ejus Synagoga superposuit in die desponsationis ejus. Tunc enim universam Ecclesiam sibi despondit, quando in patibulum crucis ascendens, ex eadem cruce signum in frontibus omnes in se credentes edocuit, sicut ipse ait: Ego cum exaltatus fuero a terra, traham omnia ad meipsum (Joan. XII) . Qui dies passionis fuit etiam dies laetitiae cordis ejus: sicut enim Christus quae bona per suam possessionem, in progenies, et multa tempora fidelibus condonavit.
chunks.english: “Go out and see, daughters of Zion.” Holy souls, always keep before your eyes King Solomon—our peace-maker, who is Christ. See how he endured his passion, as the Gospel of Mark, chapter fifteen, and the Gospel of John, chapter nineteen, proclaim, so that he might free the human race from destruction. Look at him “in the diadem with which his mother crowned him”: that is, in the crown of thorns which the synagogue placed upon his head on the day of his betrothal. For he betrothed the whole Church to himself at the moment when he ascended the gibbet of the cross and, from that same cross, taught all who believe in him the sign to place upon their foreheads. As he himself says in the Gospel of John, chapter twelve: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself.” That day of his passion was also the day of his heart’s joy, because through his suffering Christ granted good things to the faithful as his own possession, for generations and for many ages.
chunks.notes: The final Latin sentence appears compressed or textually rough; the translation gives the likely sense, connecting Christ’s passion with the blessings granted to believers across time. The final Latin sentence as printed (“sicut enim Christus quae bona per suam possessionem, in progenies, et multa tempora fidelibus condonavit”) is incomplete; the rendering is a conjectural completion of its evident drift and should not be cited as the text.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Christ Praises the Church's Beauty and Gifts
chunks.latin: CAP. IV.
chunks.english: Chapter 4: Christ Praises the Church's Beauty and Gifts

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 70. Quam pulchra es, amica mea. Repetitio sermonis commendat pulchritudinem quam laudat; vel ea sanctorum genera quae sub specie similitudinum intromittit, consideranda praemonstrat.
chunks.english: “How beautiful you are, my friend.” By repeating the phrase, Christ emphasizes the beauty he is praising. Or else, by using these images, he is signaling that we should carefully consider the different kinds of holy people that he is about to introduce under these comparisons.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 71. Oculi columbarum absque eo. Simplicitas spiritualium plurimum veneranda, quia se nec extollere noverunt, et conscia puritate magis Deo quam hominibus placere contendunt.
chunks.english: “Your eyes are those of doves, apart from what lies within.” The simplicity of spiritual people deserves the deepest reverence, because they do not know how to exalt themselves. Conscious of their purity, they strive to please God more than human beings.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 72. Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum. Docet Apostolus mulieri capillos pro ornamento datos (I Cor. XI) ; et idcirco Ecclesia illos populos in ornamento quam maxime habet, qui ex circumcisione primitius crediderunt, qui venditis et in usum pauperum prorogatis facultatibus suis habebant cor unum et animam unam (Act. IV) . Hi ascenderunt de monte Galaad: Galaad interpretatur, acervus testimonii, ac si ascensus, id est profectus eorum processit de testimoniis sanctarum Scripturarum, cum illic Christum intellexerunt in quem postea crediderunt.
chunks.english: “Your hair is like flocks of goats.” The Apostle teaches, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, that hair was given to a woman as an adornment. So the Church especially counts as her adornment those peoples who first believed from among the circumcised. They sold their possessions, distributed the proceeds for the use of the poor, and had one heart and one soul, as Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter four. These came up from Mount Gilead. Gilead means “heap of testimony.” In other words, their ascent—that is, their spiritual progress—came from the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, because in those Scriptures they recognized the Christ in whom they later believed.
chunks.notes: Gilead is interpreted allegorically from its Hebrew meaning as a place of testimony.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 73. Dentes tui sicut greges detonsarum. Dentes, praedicatores dicit, qui ea quae susceperunt, salubriter comminuendum, in corpus Christi trajiciunt. Hi detonsarum gregibus comparantur, quia deposito vetere homine, in novitate Spiritus processerunt. Ascenderunt quoque de lavacro, cum accepta per baptismata remissione peccatorum profecerunt in Christo.
chunks.english: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep.” By teeth he means preachers. They take what they have received, break it down in a saving way, and pass it into the body of Christ. These preachers are compared to flocks of shorn sheep because they have put off the old self and have moved forward in the newness of the Spirit. They have also come up from the washing, because, after receiving forgiveness of sins through baptism, they made progress in Christ.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 74. Omnes gemellis fetibus. Omnes repleti in charitate Christi et proximi, et quia ad misericordiam prompti, idcirco sterilis nemo inter eos (Jos. VI) .
chunks.english: “All of them bear twins.” All are filled with love for Christ and for their neighbor. And because they are ready for mercy, none among them is barren, as the Book of Joshua, chapter six, is understood to suggest.
chunks.notes: The connection with Joshua chapter six is not explicit in the lemma; it may be linked to the following discussion of Rahab.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 75. Sicut vitta coccinea labia tua. Raab illa meretrix quae salvari meruit et Israelitico populo associari, coccineum funiculum in signum salutis per fenestram suae domus appendit. Quapropter illorum labia decora, quia passionem igitur praedicant, et per ejus sanguinem datam redemptionem annuntiant; nihilque dulcius quod loquantur se invenisse congaudent, sicut et Apostolus ait: Nihil me arbitror inter vos scire, nisi Christum Jesum, et hunc crucifixum (I Cor. I) .
chunks.english: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon.” Rahab, the prostitute who was found worthy to be saved and joined to the people of Israel, hung a scarlet cord from the window of her house as a sign of salvation. Therefore their lips are beautiful, because they preach the passion and announce the redemption given through his blood. They rejoice that they have found nothing sweeter to speak about. As the Apostle says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter one: “I judge that I know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”
chunks.notes: The Latin citation gives First Corinthians chapter one, though the wording corresponds to First Corinthians chapter two, verse two in modern numbering.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 76. Sicut fragmen mali punici genae. Illi in facie Ecclesiae decorem efficiunt, qui, comitante verecundia, castitatem observant; sive sancti martyres, qui, imitantes Christi passionem, roseo sanguinis sui decore perfusi sunt, absque eo quod intrinsecus latet, praeter castitatis et martyrii meritum. Multa sunt et alia sanctorum bona quae ille novit quia ea in eorum corde concessit.
chunks.english: “Your cheeks are like a slice of pomegranate.” Those who preserve chastity, with modesty as its companion, create beauty in the face of the Church. So do the holy martyrs: by imitating Christ’s passion, they are covered with the rosy beauty of their own blood. And this is only the visible beauty; besides the merit of chastity and martyrdom, there is also what lies hidden within. The saints possess many other good things, known to Christ, because he himself granted them in their hearts.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 77. Sicut turris David collum tuum. Turris dicitur perfectio vel doctrina sanctorum, quae non a se, sed a Christo aedificata est cum propugnaculis, cum sanctarum Scripturarum testimoniis, quibus infideles vel haeretici debellantur.
chunks.english: “Your neck is like the tower of David.” The tower means the perfection or the teaching of the saints. It was not built by them, but by Christ. It has its defenses: the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, by which unbelievers and heretics are defeated.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 78. Mille clypei pendent. Potest haec turris, Scriptura canonica Veteris et Novi Testamenti convenienter intelligi, quae per Spiritum sanctum velut turris excelsa, constructa est. Mille clypei pendent ex ea. Hic numerus per plenitudinem universitatis accipitur, sicut in Psalmo: Verbi quod mandavit in mille generationibus (Psalm. CIV) , tanquam diceret, in omnes generationes. Itaque in hac sancta Scriptura, omnis armatura fortium reperitur; ex qua vel contra diabolum, vel contra ministros ejus fortiter repugnatur. Nam et ipse Dominus, cum in deserto a diabolo tentaretur (Matth. IV) , ex hac turri arma produxit, cum eum prolatis ex sacra Scriptura testimoniis usquequaque devicit.
chunks.english: “A thousand shields hang from it.” This tower can fittingly be understood as the canonical Scripture of the Old and New Testaments, constructed by the Holy Spirit like a lofty tower. “A thousand shields hang from it.” This number is taken as a sign of complete fullness. So the Psalm says, in Psalm one hundred four, “the word that he commanded for a thousand generations,” meaning, as it were, for all generations. Therefore every weapon of the strong is found in holy Scripture. From it one fights powerfully against the devil and against the devil’s servants. Indeed, when the Lord himself was tempted by the devil in the desert, as the Gospel of Matthew, chapter four, recounts, he drew weapons from this tower: by bringing forward testimonies from sacred Scripture, he defeated the devil completely.
chunks.notes: Psalm numbering follows the Latin tradition; many modern Bibles number this as Psalm one hundred five.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 79. Duo ubera sicut duo hinnuli capreae. Duo ubera Ecclesiae duo sunt Testamenta coaptata duobus hinnulis capreae gemellis, id est duobus populis qui ex te nutriuntur, circumcisionis videlicet et praeputii, ex peccati traduce natis; quae tamen pascuntur in liliis, dum sanctorum proficiunt pariter exemplis et doctrinis.
chunks.english: “Your two breasts are like two young fawns, twins of a gazelle.” The two breasts of the Church are the two Testaments. They are fitted to the two twin fawns—that is, to the two peoples who are nourished from you: the people of the circumcision and the people of the foreskin. Both were born from the inheritance of sin. Yet they feed among the lilies when they grow together through the examples and teachings of the saints.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 80. Donec aspiret dies, et inclinetur. Donec, sicut Apostolus ait, absorbeatur quod mortale est (II Cor. V) .
chunks.english: “Until the day breathes, and turns.” This means: until, as the Apostle says in Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter five, what is mortal is swallowed up.
chunks.notes: The printed lemma is abbreviated: “Donec aspiret dies, et inclinetur” (Vulgate: “et inclinentur umbrae”); the translation renders what is printed.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 81. Vadam ad montem myrrhae. Conjungar his qui se propter Deum mortificando creverunt, seque illi offerendo odorem gratiae propinare non desinunt.
chunks.english: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh.” That is: I will be joined to those who have grown by putting themselves to death for God’s sake, and who never cease, by offering themselves to him, to pour out the fragrance of grace.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 82. Tota pulchra es, amica mea. Sicut dicit Apostolus, ut exhiberet sibi Ecclesiam sine macula et ruga (Ephes. III) . Nec hoc vacat quod ait, Tota pulchra es, in omnibus scilicet pusillis et magnis. Sed sic, non solum in martyribus, confessoribus, eruditis virginibus, sed etiam in continentibus, eleemosynariis ac poenitentibus.
chunks.english: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend.” As the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, cited here as chapter three, Christ desired to present the Church to himself without spot or wrinkle. Nor is it meaningless that he says, “You are wholly beautiful.” He means: in all her members, small and great. Not only in martyrs, confessors, and learned virgins, but also in the continent, in those who give alms, and in penitents.
chunks.notes: The Latin citation gives Ephesians chapter three, but the wording corresponds to Ephesians chapter five, verse twenty-seven in modern numbering.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 83. Veni de Libano, sponsa mea, veni. Libanus candor interpretatur: nisi enim quis candorem sacro baptismate quo peccatorum remissio datur, perceperit, ad Christum venire non potest.
chunks.english: “Come from Lebanon, my bride, come.” Lebanon is interpreted as “whiteness.” Unless a person receives that whiteness through holy baptism, where forgiveness of sins is given, that person cannot come to Christ.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 84. Coronaberis de capite Amana. Seir interpretatur lucerna; Hermon consecratio: quae omnia referuntur ad Christum, qui quos illuminat, consecrat, ipsosque coronat, quos illuminans consecraverit.
chunks.english: “You will be crowned from the summit of Amana.” Seir is interpreted as “lamp,” and Hermon as “consecration.” All these meanings refer to Christ. Those whom he enlightens, he consecrates; and those whom he enlightens and consecrates, he also crowns.
chunks.notes: The Song’s place-names are treated through traditional etymological interpretation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 85. De cubilibus leonum. Evocatur Ecclesia de cubilibus leonum et montibus pardorum, quando relicta elatione superba vel diversarum traditione sectarum simplex et humilis venit ad Christum.
chunks.english: “From the dens of lions.” The Church is called out from the dens of lions and from the mountains of leopards when, leaving behind proud self-exaltation and the traditions of various sects, she comes to Christ simple and humble.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 86. Vulnerasti cor meum, soror mea. Vulnus istud cordis dilectio est. Ingentis amoris itaque in illo oculo, Ecclesia Christo complacuit; quoniam non temporalia, sed aeterna prospexit. Sicque jam in uno crine colli; quia non ornari visibilibus, sed futuris studuit; aut forte unus oculus et crinis colli, est credentis Ecclesiae populus quem Christus sic dilexit, ut animam suam poneret pro eo.
chunks.english: “You have wounded my heart, my sister.” This wound of the heart is love. Therefore, with that one eye of immense love, the Church pleased Christ, because she looked ahead not to temporal things, but to eternal things. So too with the one lock of hair on her neck: she sought to be adorned not with visible things, but with things to come. Or perhaps the one eye and the lock of hair on the neck mean the believing people of the Church, whom Christ loved so much that he laid down his life for them.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 87. Quam pulchrae sunt mammae tuae. Quam admirandi sunt illi doctores qui nascentes in fide homines nutriunt, et garrientium carnalium molestias populorum tanquam piae nutrices perferunt, donec quos spirituali lacte educaverint, ad perfectionem perducant.
chunks.english: “How beautiful are your breasts.” How worthy of admiration are those teachers who nourish people newly born in faith. Like devoted nurses, they endure the troubles caused by chattering, fleshly crowds, until they lead to maturity those whom they have raised on spiritual milk.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 88. Pulchriora ubera tua vino. Jam supra, ubera ista apostolos, vel apostolicos viros esse praediximus, quorum doctrina vinum exuberat: veteris scilicet legis traditionem atque praeceptum. Et odor unguentorum tuorum super omnia aromata. Distributio gratiarum quae per Spiritum sanctum concessa est, quam Apostolus declarat cum dicit: alii datur sermo sapientiae, alii scientiae (I Cor., XII) etc., in tantum praeeminet, ut cunctas mundi vanitates exsuperet.
chunks.english: “Your breasts are more beautiful than wine.” As mentioned earlier, these breasts are the apostles, or apostolic men. Their teaching surpasses the wine—that is, the tradition and commandment of the old law. “And the fragrance of your ointments is beyond all spices.” This means the distribution of graces granted through the Holy Spirit. The Apostle explains it in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter twelve, when he says, “To one is given a word of wisdom, to another a word of knowledge,” and so on. This grace is so excellent that it surpasses all the vanities of the world.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 89. Favus distillans labia tua, sponsa. Favus distillans labia tua, expositio Scripturarum sacrarum, mel et lac in doctrina tua, sub lingua tua, eo quod lacte parvulos nutris, et in melle diversorum vulnerum sive peccatorum putredines tollis.
chunks.english: “Your lips, my bride, are a dripping honeycomb.” The dripping honeycomb of your lips is the exposition of the sacred Scriptures. “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” that is, in your teaching: with milk you nourish the little ones, and with honey you remove the rottenness of various wounds, that is, of sins.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 90. Et odor vestimentorum tuorum. Dicit per prophetam ad Jerusalem de sanctis: Vivo ego, dicit Dominus, quia omnibus his velut ornamento vestieris et circumdabis tibi eos quasi sponsa. Proinde vestimenta Ecclesiae, omnes videlicet sancti praeclari in verbis et operibus, reddunt suavitatem odoris.
chunks.english: “And the fragrance of your garments.” Through the prophet, the Lord speaks to Jerusalem about the saints: “As I live, says the Lord, you will be clothed with all these as with an ornament, and you will wrap them around yourself like a bride.” Therefore the garments of the Church are all the saints, resplendent in words and works; and they give off a sweet fragrance.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 91. Hortus conclusus soror mea sponsa. Huic sponsae, quae velut hortus concluditur, id est Christi gratia, tam indissolubili materia circumdatur, ut de ea Isaias propheta dixerit: Non adjiciet ut pertranseat per te omnis incircumcisus et immundus (Isa. LII) . Potest etiam hortus conclusus et fons signatus, ipsa mater Domini S. Maria intelligi, quae virgo concipiens virgoque generans, conclusi horti et signati fontis intemeratum in se decus exhibuit.
chunks.english: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride.” This bride is enclosed like a garden; that is, by the grace of Christ she is surrounded with such an unbreakable enclosure that the prophet Isaiah says of her, in Isaiah, chapter fifty-two: “No uncircumcised or unclean person will ever again pass through you.” The enclosed garden and sealed fountain can also be understood as the Lord’s own mother, Saint Mary. Conceiving as a virgin and giving birth as a virgin, she displayed in herself the undefiled beauty of an enclosed garden and a sealed fountain.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 92. Emissiones tuae paradisus malorum. Profectus tui, congregatio sanctorum martyrum, cum pomorum fructibus; cum reliqua fidelium multitudine quae justitiae dulcedine decoratur.
chunks.english: “Your shoots are a paradise of apple trees.” Your growth means the gathering of the holy martyrs, together with the fruits of the trees; that is, together with the rest of the faithful multitude, adorned with the sweetness of righteousness.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 93. Cypri cum nardo, nardus et crocus. Incorruptio et fortitudo virtutis martyrum, doctrina, bona fama, reperiuntur in universis populis baptismate in Christo renatis.
chunks.english: “Henna with nard, nard and saffron.” The incorruption and strong virtue of the martyrs, along with teaching and good reputation, are found among all peoples reborn in Christ through baptism.
chunks.notes: Cyprus or cyprus-flower is rendered here as henna, the usual plant meant in the Song of Songs.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 94. Myrrha ex aloe cum omnibus. Mortis Christi insignia cum praecipuis S. Spiritus donis.
chunks.english: “Myrrh and aloes, with all the finest spices.” These are the signs of Christ’s death, together with the chief gifts of the Holy Spirit.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 95. Fons hortorum, puteus aquarum. Fons patens eruditio populorum; puteus, profunditas doctrinarum; quae fluunt impetu de Libano, cum fervore Spiritus emittuntur a Christo.
chunks.english: “A fountain of gardens, a well of waters.” The open fountain is the instruction of peoples. The well is the depth of doctrines. These waters flow with force from Lebanon when they are sent out by Christ with the fervor of the Spirit.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 96. Surge, Aquilo, et veni, Auster. Unus Spiritus, id est, quia Aquilo atque Auster sunt diversa vocabula, unius Spiritus sancti insinuat dona, Aquilo dum aestuantibus refrigeria praebet, Auster dum duros ad credendum vel benefaciendum resolvit. Aquilonem autem in bonam partem poni Psalmista docet, Mons Sion latera Aquilonis civitas Regis magni (Psal. XLVII) . Et rursum Ezechiel propheta: Est super me manus Domini, et vidi, et ecce Spiritus fulgens veniebat ab Aquilone (Ezech. I) . Et quoniam in duobus unus advertitur, non ait, Perflate, sed Perfla hortum meum, et fluant aromata illius: inspira credentem populum, et redundent bona opera ejus.
chunks.english: “Rise up, North Wind, and come, South Wind.” There is one Spirit. Although North Wind and South Wind are different names, the text is pointing to the gifts of the one Holy Spirit. He is called the North Wind when he gives coolness to those who are burning with heat; he is called the South Wind when he softens those who are hard, so that they may believe and do good. The Psalmist teaches that the North Wind can be understood in a good sense when he says, in Psalm forty-seven: “Mount Zion, the sides of the north, the city of the great King.” And again the prophet Ezekiel says, in Ezekiel, chapter one: “The hand of the Lord was upon me, and I looked, and behold, a shining Spirit was coming from the north.” And because one Spirit is recognized in the two winds, the text does not say in the plural, “Blow, you winds,” but in the singular, “Breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow.” In other words: inspire the believing people, and let their good works abound.
chunks.notes: The translation preserves the author’s grammatical point: the Latin imperative is singular, supporting the allegory of one Holy Spirit under two names.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Christ Enters the Church and Sustains His Bride
chunks.latin: CAP. V.
chunks.english: Chapter 5: Christ Enters the Church and Sustains His Bride

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 97. Veniat dilectus meus in hortum suum. Ingrediatur in Ecclesiam suam et delectetur in operibus sanctorum suorum; vel, pascatur a fidelibus in pauperibus, retributurus pro temporalibus regnum aeternum.
chunks.english: “Let my beloved come into his garden.” That is: let him enter his Church, and take delight in the works of his saints. Or again: let him be fed by the faithful in the persons of the poor, since he will repay these temporary acts of mercy with the eternal kingdom.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 98. Veni in hortum meum, soror mea. Festina ad regnum meum, plebs nomine meo ditata: soror mea, de sanguine meo; sponsa mea, in fide mea, sicut et Oscas propheta dicit: Desponsabo te mihi in fide (Ose. II).
chunks.english: “Come into my garden, my sister.” In other words: hurry toward my kingdom, people enriched by my name. You are my sister, because you come from my blood; you are my bride, because you belong to my faith. As the prophet Hosea says, in Hosea, chapter two: “I will betroth you to myself in faith.”
chunks.notes: The Latin has “Oscas,” evidently a scribal or printed error for Hosea.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 99. Messui myrrham meam cum aromatibus meis. Suscipe qui propter me passi vel mortui sunt, cum meritis eorum, martyres meos.
chunks.english: “I have harvested my myrrh with my spices.” That means: receive my martyrs, those who suffered or died for my sake, together with the merits that belong to them.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0979C] Num. 100. Comede favum cum melle meo. Eos qui tenera vel vehementiore doctrina Veteris et Novi Testamenti cruditi sunt, suscipe in corpore meo.
chunks.english: “Eat the honeycomb with my honey.” That is: receive into my body those who have been formed by the gentler teaching and by the stronger teaching of the Old and New Testaments.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 101. Comedite, amici, et bibite. Dicit Dominus in Evangelio ad apostolos: Jam non dico vos servos, sed amicos (Joan. XV). Petro autem apostolo in illo vase de coelis emisso in quo ei diversa genera animalium sunt ostensa, dictum est: Petre, macta et manduca (Act. X): id est, mortifica; quod sunt, et quod ipse es, effice. Ergo comedite, amici, et bibite. Sit vobis laetitia de conversatione populorum in vestram transeuntium unitatem.
chunks.english: “Eat, friends, and drink.” In the Gospel, the Lord says to the apostles, in the Gospel of John, chapter fifteen: “I no longer call you servants, but friends.” And to the apostle Peter, when that vessel was sent down from heaven and many kinds of animals were shown to him, it was said in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter ten: “Peter, kill and eat.” In other words: put to death what they are, and make them what you yourself are. So then, “Eat, friends, and drink.” Let there be joy for you over the way of life of the peoples as they pass into your unity.
chunks.notes: “Kill and eat” is interpreted allegorically as the apostles’ work of converting the nations into the unity of the Church.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 102. Ego dormio, et cor meum vigilat. Propter Christum mori paratus sum, sed post mortem cum ipso regnaturum me esse credo. Ego etiam a temporalibus [Col. 0979D] delectationibus, consopitis quodammodo sensibus, conquiesco; sed futura desidero aeternaque conquiro.
chunks.english: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch.” I am ready to die for Christ, but I believe that after death I will reign with him. I also rest from temporary pleasures, as though my senses had been lulled to sleep; but I long for what is to come, and I seek what is eternal.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 103. Vox dilecti pulsantis. Dicit in Apocalypsi ipse Dominus: Ego sto ad ostium et pulso; si quis aperuerit mihi, introibo cum illo et coenabo cum ipso, et ipse mecum (Apoc. III). Pulsat Dominus quando quae bona sunt, vel per doctrinam docet, vel occulta inspiratione sanctorum corda ad bene faciendum instigat. Vel haec est vox pulsantis in Evangelio: Venite ad me omnes qui laboratis et onerati estis, et ego reficiam vos (Matth. XI).
chunks.english: “The voice of my beloved knocking.” The Lord himself says in the book of Revelation, chapter three: “I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens to me, I will come in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me.” The Lord knocks when he teaches what is good through doctrine, or when, by a hidden inspiration, he urges the hearts of the saints to do good. Or this may be the voice of the one knocking in the Gospel: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” as it says in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter eleven.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 104. Aperi mihi, soror mea amica mea. Aperiri sibi petit Christus, vel obedientia infidelium, vel in fide [Col. 0980A] gentium vocatarum; tunc enim ostium illi aperitur, quando ea quae praecepit adimplentur, vel quando in his qui crediderunt ei per fidem introitus reseratur. Soror Christi est Ecclesia de sanguine ejus; amica, quia per mortem ejus reconciliata; columba, de Spiritu sancto, immaculata baptismi sacramento.
chunks.english: “Open to me, my sister, my friend.” Christ asks to be opened to: either through the obedience of unbelievers brought to faith, or through the faith of the nations who have been called. The door is opened to him when the things he commanded are fulfilled, or when an entrance is unlocked for him through faith in those who have believed in him. The Church is Christ’s sister because she comes from his blood; she is his friend because she has been reconciled through his death; she is his dove because she comes from the Holy Spirit; and she is spotless through the sacrament of baptism.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 105. Quia caput meum plenum est. Hi qui principali honore in Ecclesia praeeminere videntur, quasi caput in Christi corpore advertuntur; et qui in ipsa fidelium congregatione sacramenta visibilia administrant, veluti cincinni describuntur. Sed quia plerumque mortales homines vitiis vel tenebrarum operibus inficiuntur: hi ergo velut guttis noctium praegravati, Christo quasi capiti adhaerere videntur. Sed de quibusdam Apostolus ait: Ipsi Christum non sincere annuntiant [Col. 0980B] (Philip. I). Propterea vox sponsae, velut pro talibus ingemiscentis subsequitur.
chunks.english: “For my head is full.” Those who seem to hold the highest honor in the Church are understood as a kind of head in the body of Christ. And those who administer the visible sacraments within the assembly of the faithful are described as the locks of hair. But because mortal human beings are often stained by vices and by works of darkness, such ministers seem to cling to Christ the head while weighed down, as it were, with the drops of night. About certain people like this the Apostle says, in Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter one: “They proclaim Christ insincerely.” And so the bride’s voice follows, groaning as it were for such people.
chunks.notes: The verse being interpreted is Song of Songs five, verse two, where the beloved’s head and hair are wet with the night.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 106. Spoliavi me tunica mea. Veniens ad fidem, veterem hominem secundum pristinam conversationem deposui, et indui novum, qui secundum Deum creatus est (Ephes. IV). Si quid etiam contagii dum in terrenis gradior, pedibus meis accessit, Christo lavante ablutum est; et tunc ministros sacramentorum per quos ornari debeo, carnalibus infectos vitiis non sine moerore conspicio. Et idcirco quia malis quibus renuntiaveram, in quorumdam praevaricatione me fuscari persentio, Spoliavi me tunica mea, quomodo induar illa? Lavi pedes meos, quomodo inquinabo eos? Lugubri corde pronuntio, tanquam apertius loquens: Nunquid condecet ut vestibus peccatorum quibus credens [Col. 0980C] me exui, iterum induar? Aut sordibus quibus abluta sum, rursus male vivendo inquinari me patiar? vel si oportet ut a profectu ad defectum, vel a nitore justitiae ad peccatorum nigredinem male conversando regrediar?
chunks.english: “I have taken off my tunic.” Coming to faith, I put off the old self, with its former way of life, and I put on the new self, which was created according to God, as Paul says in his letter to the Ephesians, chapter four. And if any stain clung to my feet while I walked through earthly things, it was washed away by Christ. Yet then I see, and not without sorrow, that the ministers of the sacraments, by whom I ought to be adorned, are infected with fleshly vices. Because, through the wrongdoing of certain people, I sense myself being darkened again by the very evils I had renounced, I say: “I have taken off my tunic; how can I put it on again? I have washed my feet; how can I dirty them?” With a grieving heart I speak, as if saying more plainly: Is it right for me to put on again the garments of sin from which I was stripped when I believed? Or should I allow myself to be stained again by living badly, with the filth from which I have been washed? Should I turn back, through evil conduct, from progress to decline, from the brightness of righteousness to the blackness of sins?

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 107. Dilectus meus misit manum suam. Misit manum suam per foramen, quando me per passionum angustias transire perdocuit; et venter meus conturbatus est ad tactum ejus, quando imminente persecutione infirmiores mei conturbati contremuerunt acerbitate poenarum quae mihi illatae sunt ex permissu ejus. Tactus autem iste, advenientis plagae intelligitur cruciatus, secundum illud in Job, dicente Satana ad Dominum: Alioqui tange ossa, et carnem ejus, nisi in faciem benedixerit tibi (Job I).
chunks.english: “My beloved put his hand through the opening.” He put his hand through the opening when he taught me to pass through the narrow straits of suffering. “And my inner being was disturbed at his touch”: this happened when persecution was close at hand, and my weaker members were shaken and trembled at the bitterness of the punishments inflicted on me with his permission. This “touch” is understood as the pain of a blow that is coming, according to what Satan says to the Lord in the book of Job, chapter one: “But touch his bones and his flesh, and see whether he does not curse you to your face.”
chunks.notes: The Latin citation reads “Job, chapter one,” but the wording corresponds to Job, chapter two, verse five. The Latin uses “bless” euphemistically where the sense is “curse.” The reference is spoken as printed (Job, chapter one); the quotation corresponds to Job, chapter two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0980D] Num. 108. Surrexi ut aperirem dilecto meo. Evigilans corde Christum confessa sum, nec deterrita suppliciis corporalibus in passionibus et in operibus meis, confessorum mortificatio, et in electis apparuit: In conspectu Domini mors pretiosa sanctorum (Psalm. CXXV).
chunks.english: “I rose to open to my beloved.” Awakened in heart, I confessed Christ. I was not frightened by bodily torments; instead, in my sufferings and in my deeds, the self-offering of the confessors appeared, and it appeared among the elect. As the Psalm says, in Psalm one hundred twenty-five: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”
chunks.notes: The Latin cites Psalm one hundred twenty-five, but the quoted verse is more commonly numbered as Psalm one hundred sixteen, verse fifteen, or in the Vulgate tradition Psalm one hundred fifteen, verse fifteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 109. Pessulum ostii mei aperui. Omni dubietate remota, Christo credidi, eumque ineffabili amore dilexi, et clara voce in nationibus praedicavi, atque ut mihi adesset in tribulationibus invocavi.
chunks.english: “I opened the bolt of my door.” With every doubt removed, I believed in Christ. I loved him with an inexpressible love, proclaimed him with a clear voice among the nations, and called upon him to be with me in my tribulations.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 110. At ille declinaverat. In hoc quasi declinavit atque transivit, cum me persequentibus tradidit et iniquis, et ut in meum corpus desaevirent, ipse permisit.
chunks.english: “But he had turned aside.” He seemed to turn aside and pass by when he handed me over to persecutors and wicked people, and allowed them to rage against my body.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0981A] Num. 111. Anima mea liquefacta est. Promissiones ejus audiens aestuavi desiderio, quando beatos esse qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam, quoniam ipsorum est regnum coelorum (Matth. V), eodem promittente cognovi.
chunks.english: “My soul melted.” Hearing his promises, I burned with longing when I learned from his own promise that those who suffer persecution for righteousness are blessed, because the kingdom of heaven belongs to them, as it says in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter five.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 112. Quaesivi et non inveni illum. Sic in conculcatione malignantium derelicta sum quasi auxiliator non esset; et qui ab inimicis defenderet, subvenire non posset, sicut et beatus Job in passione positus dixit: Clamo ad te et non exaudis me, et non respicis me; immutatus es mihi in crudelem, et in furore manus tuae adversaris mihi.
chunks.english: “I sought him and did not find him.” I was left so abandoned beneath the trampling of the wicked that it seemed as though there were no helper, and as though the one who could defend me from my enemies was unable to come to my aid. So also blessed Job said while he was suffering, in the book of Job, chapter thirty: “I cry to you, and you do not hear me; you do not look upon me. You have changed toward me into someone cruel, and in the fury of your hand you oppose me.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 113. Invenerunt me custodes. Comprehenderunt me saeculi potestates, qui quasi rempublicam regere noscuntur.
chunks.english: “The watchmen found me.” The powers of this world seized me: those who are known to govern, as it were, the commonwealth.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0981B] Num. 114. Percusserunt, vulnerarunt me plagis. Et suppliciis in corpore meo debacchati sunt; et onerantes vinculis, in carceribus concluserunt. Prolongantes exquisitis cruciatibus vitam nec mortem celeriter inferentes, ne faciliter ab illatis poenis exui possem.
chunks.english: “They struck me; they wounded me with blows.” They raged against my body with punishments, loaded me with chains, and shut me in prisons. By using carefully devised tortures, they prolonged my life and did not bring death quickly, so that I could not easily be released from the sufferings they inflicted.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 115. Tulerunt pallium meum. Etenim quando ecclesias ad solum usque demoliti sunt, et altaria simul cum Evangeliis et caeteris libris canonicis, ignibus cremaverunt; quando sacerdotes concluserunt ad metalla condemnatos, quando nec sacrificand locus, nec baptizandi libertas, nec communicandi est attributa licentia; cum haec omnia perse utores agerent, tunc quodammodo sponsae Christi, id est Ecclesiae, quasi quoddam pallium abstulerunt.
chunks.english: “They took away my cloak.” For when they demolished churches down to the ground; when they burned the altars, together with the Gospels and the other canonical books; when they imprisoned priests and condemned them to the mines; when no place was allowed for offering sacrifice, no freedom for baptizing, and no permission for giving or receiving communion—when the persecutors did all these things, then in a sense they took away a kind of cloak from the bride of Christ, that is, from the Church.
chunks.notes: The Latin text has a spacing error in “perse utores,” corrected in translation as “persecutors.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 116. Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem. Sanctos [Col. 0981C] quosque conjurat si per istas tribulationes, ad ipsum, contempta vita mundi, perveniant: ut insinuent Ecclesiam in his persecutionibus constitutam, ineffabili circa Deum dilectione ferventem, nec tantis et tam horrendis angustiis ullo modo frigescentem.
chunks.english: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” She solemnly charges all the saints: if, through these tribulations and by despising the life of this world, they come to him, they are to make known that the Church, even while placed in these persecutions, burns with an indescribable love for God and is in no way cooled by such great and horrifying distress.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 117. Qualis est dilectus tuus? Vox interrogantium electorum, et fidem Ecclesiae ex ejus responsione inquirentium. Qualis est dilectus tuus ex dilecto? id est, qualis est Deus ex Deo, vel Filius a Patre? in similitudine omnium aequalitatem declarans personarum. Qui enim non discernuntur in unius esse naturae, et in eadem permanere creduntur gloria majestatis.
chunks.english: “What is your beloved?” This is the voice of the elect who ask the question and seek to learn the faith of the Church from her answer. “What is your beloved, from the Beloved?” That is: what is God from God, or the Son from the Father? By this likeness he declares the equality of all the persons. For those who are not distinguished from one another are believed to be of one nature and to remain in the same glory of majesty.
chunks.notes: The interpretation reads the Song’s comparative phrase “beloved from beloved” as a confession of the Son’s divine origin from the Father.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 118. Dilectus candidus et rubicundus. Candidus quia in principio erat Verbum, et Deus erat Verbum [Col. 0981D] (Joan. I). Rubicundus, quia ex Virgine genitus, Verbum caro factum est, et habitavit in nobis. Candidus in virginitate, rubicundus in passione: sicut et propheta de eodem dicit: Quis est iste qui venit de Edom, tinctis vestibus de Bosra (Isa. LXIII)? Edom, sanguis interpretatur; et idcirco ab effusione sanguinis rubicundus. Iste formosus in stola sua gradiens in multitudine fortitudinis suae. Electus ex millibus. Ipse est de quo in Psalmis: Quis similis erit Deo inter filios Dei (Psal. XLIV)? et iterum, Speciosus forma prae filiis hominum, diffusa est gratia in labiis tuis.
chunks.english: “My beloved is radiant and ruddy.” He is radiant because, as the Gospel of John says in chapter one: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was God.” He is ruddy because, born from the Virgin, “the Word became flesh and lived among us,” as the Gospel of John says in chapter one. He is radiant in virginity and ruddy in his Passion, just as the prophet says of him in Isaiah, chapter sixty-three: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?” Edom is interpreted here as “blood,” and so he is ruddy from the shedding of blood. “He is beautiful in his robe, walking in the greatness of his strength.” He is “chosen from thousands.” He is the one of whom the Psalms say, in Psalm forty-four: “Who will be like God among the sons of God?” And again: “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace has been poured upon your lips.”
chunks.notes: The phrase “Who will be like God among the sons of God?” is not from Psalm forty-four in standard numbering, though the following quotation, “You are beautiful in form,” is associated with Psalm forty-four in the Vulgate tradition, Psalm forty-five in many English Bibles. The etymology “Edom means blood” reflects the author’s allegorical usage; linguistically Edom is more directly connected with “red.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 119. Caput ejus aurum optimum. Legimus in Apostolo: Caput viri Christus, caput autem mulieris vir, caput vero Christi Deus (I Cor. I). Et ideo sicut in metallis [Col. 0982A] nihil simile auro, ita nec in creaturis quidquam comparabitur Creatori. Est autem caput Christi Deus, secundum quod paulo ante ex Evangelio commemoravimus, In principio erat Verbum, etc.
chunks.english: “His head is the finest gold.” We read in the Apostle, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter one: “The head of the man is Christ, the head of the woman is the man, and the head of Christ is God.” Therefore, just as among metals nothing is like gold, so among created things nothing can be compared with the Creator. God is the head of Christ according to what we recalled shortly before from the Gospel: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so on.
chunks.notes: The Latin citation reads “Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter one,” but the quotation is from chapter eleven, verse three.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 120. Comae ejus sicut elatae palmarum. Hi equidem sancti capiti suo, id est Christo, adhaerere noscuntur qui, in similitudine corvi, se peccatores agnoscunt: de quibus est ille qui dicit: Si justum me voluerim facere coram te, os meum condemnabit me (Job. IX). Et rursum alius: Quoniam iniquitatem ego agnosco (Ps. L). Et consona voce Joannes cum electis pronuntiat: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos seducimus, et veritas in nobis non est, si vero confessi fuerimus peccata nostra, fidelis et justus est qui nobis peccata dimittat et mundet nos ab omni iniquitate (I Joan. I). Similiter et Paulus: Christus Jesus venit in hunc mundum peccatores salvos facere, quorum primus ego sum (I Tim. I). Et quia omnis, secundum Evangelium, qui se humiliat et exaltabitur (Matth. XXIII; Luc. IV, XVIII): hi qui se confessione peccati dejiciunt, secundum quod in hoc libro scribitur, palmarum proceritati non immerito comparantur.
chunks.english: “His hair is like the tall branches of palm trees.” These saints are known to cling to their head, that is, to Christ, because, like the raven, they recognize that they are sinners. One of them says, as Scripture says in the book of Job, chapter nine: “If I wanted to make myself righteous before you, my own mouth would condemn me.” And another says, in Psalm fifty: “I know my iniquity.” John, speaking with the elect in one harmonious voice, declares in his first letter, chapter one: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, so that he forgives us our sins and cleanses us from every injustice.” Paul says the same in his first letter to Timothy, chapter one: “Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners, and I am the first of them.” And because, according to the Gospel—in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-three, and the Gospel of Luke, chapter four and chapter eighteen—everyone who humbles himself will be exalted, these people who lower themselves by confessing their sins are rightly compared, as this book says, to the height of palm trees.
chunks.notes: The closing Gospel reference is textually confused in the Latin. The saying occurs clearly in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-three, verse twelve, and in the Gospel of Luke, chapter fourteen, verse eleven and chapter eighteen, verse fourteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 121. Oculi ejus sicut columbae. Spiritu sancto repleti, electi ejus absque ullo felle amaritudinis permanent, et Scripturarum rivulis populum imbuunt.
chunks.english: “His eyes are like doves.” His chosen ones, filled with the Holy Spirit, remain free from every bitterness of resentment, and they nourish the people with the flowing streams of Scripture.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 122. Quae lacte sunt lotae. Exind mundiores effecti, quia Christum in carne natum, fide non dubia credunt; et sacramento visibili se renatos, ablutos et nutritos agnoscunt, resident juxta fluenta plenissima, id est inter sancti Spiritus affluentissima dona.
chunks.english: “They have been washed in milk.” They are made purer because, with unhesitating faith, they believe that Christ was born in the flesh. They also recognize that through the visible sacrament they have been reborn, washed, and nourished. So they “sit beside the fullest streams,” that is, among the most abundant gifts of the Holy Spirit.
chunks.notes: The visible sacrament here is baptism, understood as cleansing, rebirth, and nourishment in the life of the Church.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 123. Genae illius sicut areolae aromatum. Sicut enim in oculis columbarum, jure apostolos accipimus Spiritu sancto repletos, ita et in genis quae vicinae sunt oculis, eas Ecclesias quae per apostolos crediderunt quae velut areolae aromatum, suavissimum odorem ex sancta conversatione producunt: consitae a pigmentariis: piis scilicet praedicatoribus, ad quos Apostolus ait: Tu autem cum oleaster esses, insertus es in illis, et socius radicis et pinguedinis olivae factus es (Rom. XI).
chunks.english: “His cheeks are like beds of spices.” In the dove-like eyes, we rightly understand the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit. So too, in the cheeks, which are close to the eyes, we understand the churches that came to faith through the apostles. Like beds of spices, these churches give off a most pleasant fragrance through holy conduct. They were planted by perfumers, that is, by devout preachers. To such people the Apostle says, in his letter to the Romans, chapter eleven: “You, although you were a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among them, and became a partner in the root and richness of the olive tree.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 124. Labia illius distillantia myrrham. Doctores ejus Spiritu vel etiam carne Virginis; in hocque passionem ejus praedicantes, ut pro illo qui pro nobis mortuus est non recusent mortem.
chunks.english: “His lips drip myrrh.” His lips are his teachers, who proclaim him born of the Spirit and also of the flesh of the Virgin, and who in this myrrh preach his passion, so that, for the sake of the one who died for us, they themselves will not refuse death.
chunks.notes: The Latin is compressed and possibly corrupt. The translation makes explicit the likely theological sense: the teachers confess both Christ’s incarnation from the Virgin and his passion, symbolized by myrrh.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 125. Manus illius tornatiles aureae. In manibus Christi deputantur qui ea quae bona sunt operari non desinunt. Idcirco tornatiles aureae, quia ad omne opus bonum semper paratae; plenae hyacinthis, secundum illud Apostoli: Divites in operibus bonis, facile tribuentes, et thesaurizantes sibi fundamentum bonum in futuro, ut apprehendant veram vitam (I Tim. VI).
chunks.english: “His hands are golden and rounded.” Those who never cease doing what is good are counted as the hands of Christ. They are called rounded and golden because they are always ready for every good work. They are “full of jacinths,” in keeping with the Apostle’s words in his first letter to Timothy, chapter six: “Be rich in good works, generous in giving, storing up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life.”
chunks.notes: “Jacinths” translates hyacinthis, a precious blue stone in ancient gem terminology.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 126. Venter ejus eburneus. In ventre ipsius deputantur, qui credentes in fide parturiunt; et eburneus etiam ipse venter, fons baptismi ex quo renascimur non inconvenienter accipitur; et quia eboris, defuncti animantis speciosa et incorruptibilia ossa noscuntur, propterea nobis ab Apostolo dicitur: An ignoratis quia quicunque baptizati sumus in Christo Jesu, in morte ipsius baptizati sumus? Consepulti enim sumus cum illo in baptismum per mortem, ut quomodo surrexit Christus per gloriam Patris, ita et nos in novitate vitae ambulemus (Gal. III). Distinctus sapphiris; adornatus ex se progenitis et in confessione clarissimis sanctis.
chunks.english: “His belly is ivory.” Those who bring believers to birth in faith are counted as his belly. And the ivory belly may also quite fittingly be understood as the fountain of baptism, from which we are reborn. Ivory, after all, is known to be the beautiful and incorruptible bone of a dead animal. For this reason the Apostle says to us, in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter three: “Do you not know that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ rose through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.” “Set with sapphires” means that he is adorned with the saints born from him, saints who shine most brightly in their confession of faith.
chunks.notes: The Latin cites Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter three, but the quotation is from Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter six, verses three through four. The opening phrase resembles Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter three, verse twenty-seven.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 127. Crura illius columnae marmoreae. Crura quae totum corpus bajulant, ipsi sunt sancti qui domum Ecclesiae, et velut marmoreae columnae fundatae super bases aureas describuntur. Hi enim justi qui caeteros charitate supportant, et Scripturarum consolationibus fulciunt, sicut ait Apostolus: Debemus nos firmiores imbecillitatem infirmorum sustinere, et non nobis placere. Et paulo post, tanquam bases aureas Scripturas sanctas insinuat dicens: Quaecunque scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, ut per patientiam et consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus (Rom. XV).
chunks.english: “His legs are marble columns.” The legs that carry the whole body are the saints themselves. They are described as supporting the house of the Church, like marble columns set upon golden bases. These are the righteous who bear up others through love and strengthen them with the encouragement of the Scriptures. As the Apostle says in his letter to the Romans, chapter fifteen: “We who are stronger ought to bear the weakness of the weak, and not please ourselves.” A little later, he points to the holy Scriptures as the golden bases, saying: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 128. Species ejus ut Libani, electus ut cedri. Omnes sancti qui suavissimum odorem ex bona conversatione dederunt, et in corruptionis integritate perdurant, Deo auctore, tantorum bonorum gratiam perceperunt.
chunks.english: “His appearance is like Lebanon, choice as the cedars.” All the saints who have given off the sweetest fragrance through good conduct, and who remain whole and uncorrupted, have received the grace of such great blessings from God as their author.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 129. Guttur illius suavissimum. Hi qui mysteria ejus exponunt, et in lege ipsius quotidie meditantur, in sacra doctrina saporem suavissimum administrant. Et totus desiderabilis. Ubi illud adimplebitur quod B. Joan. in Epistola sua dicit: Charissimi, nunc filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quod erimus. Scimus quia cum apparuerit, similes ei erimus et videbimus eum sicuti est (I Joan. III).
chunks.english: “His throat is most sweet.” Those who explain his mysteries and meditate daily on his law provide, in sacred teaching, a most delightful taste. “And he is altogether desirable.” Then will be fulfilled what blessed John says in his first letter, chapter three: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, and we shall see him as he is.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 130. Talis est dilectus meus. Ad has gratiarum varietates, et ad ista mysteriorum ornamenta justos intendere persuadet, cum sponsi decorem in ejus membris contemplandum insinuat.
chunks.english: “Such is my beloved.” She urges the righteous to give their attention to this variety of graces and to these adornments of the mysteries, when she suggests that the bridegroom’s beauty should be contemplated in his members.
chunks.notes: “His members” means the faithful who belong to Christ’s body, the Church.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 131. Quo abiit dilectus tuus? Tanquam scrutantes atque dicentes: Quia tantam pulchritudinem ejus exposuisti, ut ad quaerendum eum, nostrum cor ardens efficeretur, nunc ostende quo abierit, vel ubi declinaverit. Bene autem appellatur Ecclesia virgo, pulcherrima mulierum, quia de ea Paulus sic fidelibus loquitur: Despondi vos uni viro, ut virginem castam exhiberem Christo (I Cor. XI). Et congrue de ipso dicunt: Quo abiit, quo declinavit dilectus tuus. Declinavit enim quodammodo cum in forma Dei esset, et non rapinam arbitratus est esse se aequalem Deo, sed semetipsum exinanivit formam servi accipiens, in similitudinem hominum factus et habitu inventus ut homo; humiliavit se usque ad mortem, mortem autem crucis (Philip. II). Igitur qui excelsum quaesierit in forma Dei, non eum reperiet nisi credat in formam servi: in qua se idcirco humiliavit, ut nos jacentes erigeret.
