chunks.english: “Where has your beloved gone?” They speak as people searching, as if saying: “You have described such great beauty in him that our hearts have been set on fire to seek him. Now show us where he has gone, or where he has turned aside.” The Church is rightly called a virgin, “the most beautiful of women,” because Paul speaks to the faithful about her in this way, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven: “I betrothed you to one husband, so that I might present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.” And they fittingly say of him: “Where has your beloved gone? Where has he turned aside?” For in a sense he did turn aside: although he was in the form of God and did not think equality with God something to be seized, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant. He was made in the likeness of human beings, and, being found in appearance as a man, he humbled himself even to death, death on a cross, as Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two, says. Therefore, whoever seeks the Exalted One in the form of God will not find him unless he believes in the form of a servant. He humbled himself in that form precisely so that he might raise us up as we lay fallen.
chunks.notes: The Latin cites Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, but the betrothal quotation is from Paul’s second letter to the Corinthians, chapter eleven, verse two. The Christological quotation is from Paul’s letter to the Philippians, chapter two, verses six through eight.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: Christ Visits His Garden, the Church
chunks.latin: CAP. VI.
chunks.english: Chapter 6: Christ Visits His Garden, the Church

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 132. Dilectus meus descendit ad hortum. Descendit ad hortum suum, quando visitavit in adventu suo Israel populum suum, sicut ipse ait: Non sum missus nisi ad oves quae perierunt domus Israel (Matth. X) . Areolam autem aromatis, ipsam S. Mariam Virginem intelligendam accipimus: ex ea quippe nobis ordo justitiae ortus est Dominus Jesus Christus.
chunks.english: “My beloved has gone down to his garden.” He went down to his garden when, at his coming, he visited Israel, his own people. As he himself says in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter ten: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” And by the little bed of spices we understand the holy Virgin Mary herself. For from her there arose for us the pattern of righteousness: the Lord Jesus Christ.
chunks.notes: The cited saying is found in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter fifteen, verse twenty-four, though the Latin source gives chapter ten.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 133. Ut pascatur in hortis, et lilia colligat. [Col. 0984A] Ut regnet in gentibus, vel in Ecclesiis delectetur: ut ex eis virgines vel sanctos quosque assumat.
chunks.english: “That he may feed in the gardens and gather lilies.” That is, that he may reign among the nations, or take delight in the churches, and from them gather to himself virgins and all the holy ones.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 134. Ego dilecto meo, et dilectus meus mihi. Ego Christi regnum et ille rex meus; ego corpus ipsius et ipse caput meum. Pascitur inter lilia, cum in corde virginum requiescit, vel cum illic per gratiam, quam ipse tribuit, quotidie augetur et proficit.
chunks.english: “I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me.” I am Christ’s kingdom, and he is my king. I am his body, and he is my head. He feeds among the lilies when he rests in the hearts of virgins, or when, by the grace he himself gives, he daily grows and flourishes there.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 135. Pulchra es amica mea, pulchra, etc. Pulchra per justitiam; suavis et amica, quia semper pacifica, decora sicut Jerusalem. Dicit Dominus in Evangelio: In resurrectione non nubent neque nubentur, sed erunt sicut angeli in coelo (Matth. XII; Luc. X) . Merito autem Ecclesia, sicut Jerusalem decora describitur, cui in aeternum similitudo angelorum a Domino condonatur.
chunks.english: “You are beautiful, my friend; beautiful,” and so on. She is beautiful through righteousness. She is gentle and beloved because she is always peaceful. She is lovely like Jerusalem. The Lord says in the Gospel, in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twelve, and the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten: “In the resurrection they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, but they will be like the angels in heaven.” So the Church is rightly described as lovely like Jerusalem, since the Lord grants her the likeness of the angels forever.
chunks.notes: The resurrection saying is cited by the Latin source as the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twelve, and the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten; the standard locations are the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-two, verse thirty, and the Gospel of Luke, chapter twenty, verses thirty-four through thirty-six.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0984B] Num. 136. Terribilis sicut castrorum acies. Quanti tyranni et persecutores una cum auctore suo diabolo, conati sunt Ecclesiae virtutem dirumpere et praevalere nullo modo potuerunt. Habet enim S. Ecclesia castrorum aciem ordinatam, quando imminente Christo, nec martyres persecutio, nec virgines carnalis delectatio, nec misericordes cupiditas, nec humiles temporalis gloriae devincit ambitio.
chunks.english: “Terrible like an army drawn up for battle.” How many tyrants and persecutors, together with their author, the devil, have tried to shatter the Church’s strength—and they have never been able to prevail. For the holy Church has an ordered battle line when Christ stands over her: persecution does not conquer the martyrs, bodily pleasure does not conquer the virgins, greed does not conquer the merciful, and ambition for worldly glory does not conquer the humble.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 137. Verte oculos tuos a me, quia. Non me semper in corpore conspiciendum requiras, quem spiritu per fidem melius cernis. Idcirco etenim in coelos ascendi, ut non semper localis tibi appaream qui sic omnia (divinitatis meae praesentia) repleo, ut ubique adsim, cunctaque contineam, et a nullo loco continear.
chunks.english: “Turn your eyes away from me, for…” Do not keep asking to see me bodily, because you see me better in spirit, through faith. This is why I ascended into heaven: so that I would not always appear to you as though confined to one place. In fact, by the presence of my divinity, I fill all things in such a way that I am present everywhere, contain everything, and am contained by no place.
chunks.notes: The Latin quotation is incomplete, reflecting an abbreviated citation of the Song of Songs.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0984C] Num. 138. Capilli tui sicut greges caprarum, dentes tui sicut grex ovium quae omnes gemellis fetibus, et sterilis, etc. Sicut cortex mali punici. Hos quatuor versus, bis in hoc loco constat esse descriptos, quos Deo donante jam in superiori loco tractavimus: in quibus tamen Judaeorum et gentilium populos convertendos cum geminae dilectionis fructu praedixit, et martyrum gloriam cum eorum meritis declaravit.
chunks.english: “Your hair is like flocks of goats”; “your teeth are like a flock of sheep, all bearing twins, with none barren”; and, “like the rind of a pomegranate.” It is clear that these four verses are written here a second time. With God’s help we have already discussed them earlier. In them, however, he foretold that both Jews and Gentiles would be converted with the fruit of the twofold love, and he revealed the glory of the martyrs together with their merits.
chunks.notes: The “twofold love” refers to love of God and love of neighbor.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 139. Sexaginta sunt reginae, et octoginta concubinae. In sexagenario numero, qui ascendente senario per denarium adimpletur, omnem bonorum perfectionem quae ex legis praeceptis consummatur, agnoscimus. Quemadmodum autem ipse senarius totis suis partibus constet, breviter adverte: nam sexta pars ejus unum, tertia duo, media autem tria esse [Col. 0984D] probatur. Unum autem, et duo, et tria, sex esse quis nesciat? quod in alio numero, distributis partibus et in unum reductis, ita adimpleri difficile invenitur. Itaque reginae perfectae sanctorum animae quae non sunt peccatorum ancillae, dicuntur: sic enim scribitur. Ubi spiritus Domini, ibi libertas (I Cor. III) . Concubinae autem, quae, sicut Agar, in servitutem generant (Gal. IV) , in illis qui suscepto semine verbi Dei non spiritualia sed carnalia sapiunt, merito deputantur. Adolescentularum autem quarum non est numerus, eorum est multitudo qui quae semper sancta sunt audire parati sunt, nec tamen quae audiunt, operibus adimplere contendunt, de quibus Apostolus dicit: Semper discentes, et nunquam ad scientiam veritatis [Col. 0985A] pervenientes (I Tim. III) . Et licet ista sint genera hominum qui Christo tanquam per doctrinam ipsius sociantur, attamen quia in electis non diversitas, sed unitas commendatur, audi quid sequitur.
chunks.english: “There are sixty queens and eighty concubines.” In the number sixty, which is completed when six rises through ten, we recognize the full perfection of good things, the perfection brought to completion by the commandments of the Law. Now notice briefly how the number six is made up of all its own parts: its sixth part is one, its third part is two, and its half is three. And everyone knows that one plus two plus three makes six. It is hard to find this same result in another number, when its parts are divided up and then brought back together into one. So the “queens” are the perfect souls of the saints, souls that are not slaves of sins. As Scripture says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter three: “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.” The “concubines,” however, are those who, like Hagar, give birth into slavery, as Paul says in his letter to the Galatians, chapter four. They are rightly understood as people who have received the seed of the word of God, yet set their minds not on spiritual things but on fleshly things. And the “young women without number” are the multitude of those who are always ready to hear holy teachings, but do not make any effort to fulfill what they hear by their actions. About them the Apostle says in Paul’s first letter to Timothy, chapter three: “Always learning, and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.” And although these are different kinds of people who are joined to Christ in some way through his teaching, nevertheless, because unity rather than diversity is praised among the elect, listen to what follows.
chunks.notes: Justus uses ancient number symbolism: six is treated as a perfect number because its proper divisors, one, two, and three, add up to six. The printed citations are First Corinthians, chapter three, and First Timothy, chapter three; the quotations are Second Corinthians three, seventeen, and Second Timothy three, seven. The spoken text follows the printed references.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 140. Una est columba mea perfecta. Columba, quia simplex est, et spiritualiter sapit; perfecta, quia mundum relinquens, me magis quam temporalia aut se diligit, secundum illud: Si vis perfectus esse, vade et vende omnia quae habes et da pauperibus, et veni et sequere me (Matth. XIX) .
chunks.english: “My dove, my perfect one, is one.” She is a dove because she is simple and thinks spiritually. She is perfect because, leaving the world behind, she loves me more than temporal things and more than herself. This agrees with the Lord’s words in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter nineteen: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give it to the poor; then come and follow me.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 141. Una est matris suae electa. Matris suae coelestis Jerusalem, de qua Apostolus dicit: Quae autem sursum est Jerusalem, mater nostra est (Gal. IV) . Una est ergo illi, quia in futura beatitudine, ipsa tantummodo consociabitur illi.
chunks.english: “She is the one chosen by her mother.” Her mother is the heavenly Jerusalem, about which the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter four: “The Jerusalem above is our mother.” She is one to that mother because, in the blessedness to come, only she will be joined to her.
chunks.notes: “She” here means the Church understood as the community of the elect.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: [Col. 0985B] Num. 142. Viderunt illam filiae, et beatissimam praedicaverunt. Quae enim sanctae sunt animae, quae Ecclesiam non miris laudibus efferunt, cum etiam nec concubinae, id est carnales, in ejus praeconio sileant, quando eam invictam in martyribus et victricem in virginibus admirantur?
chunks.english: “The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed.” What holy souls would not lift up the Church with marvelous praise? Even the concubines—that is, fleshly people—are not silent in praising her, when they admire her as unconquered in the martyrs and victorious in the virgins.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 143. Quae est ista quae progreditur quasi. Consurgit quasi aurora, cum spretis tenebrarum operibus caste et sobrie vivit in conjugatis; pulchra ut luna, cum in continentibus candido nitore resplendet; electa ut sol, cum in virginibus perfectionis decore refulget, sicut illa bona terra in Evangelio, quae suscepto in se semine verbi Dei, tricesimum et sexagesimum atque centesimum fructum produxit; terribilis ut acies ordinata. An non terribilis quae gentium [Col. 0985C] ritus idolorumque cultus subvertit, et ipsa in fide Christi perdurans, a gentibus superari non potuit? Est et in eo terribilis multum, cum ei in Petro datur illa potestas ubi dicitur: Quaecunque ligaveris super terram, erunt ligata et in coelo; et quaecunque solveris super terram, erunt soluta et in coelo (Matth. XVI et XVIII) .
chunks.english: “Who is this who comes forth like…” She rises like the dawn when, among the married, she despises the works of darkness and lives chastely and soberly. She is beautiful as the moon when, among the continent, she shines with bright radiance. She is chosen as the sun when, among virgins, she gleams with the beauty of perfection. She is like the good soil in the Gospel, which received the seed of the word of God and produced fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold. She is “terrible as an army drawn up in order.” Is she not terrible—she who overthrew the rites of the nations and the worship of idols, and, persevering in the faith of Christ, could not be overcome by the nations? She is also very terrible in this: in Peter, she is given the power described in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter sixteen, and again in chapter eighteen: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”
chunks.notes: Justus reads the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruit as married chastity, continence, and virginity.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 144. Descendi ad hortum nucum, ut viderem. Hortus nucum, canonem Veteris et Novi Testamenti designat: species enim nucum aliud ostendit in cortice, et aliud retinet in medulla. Quod si quis in Scripturis sanctis non discreverit, et quodammodo velut in nucis corticibus interna non quaesierit, et ad partum spiritualis intelligentiae pervenire non potest. Quod autem ait, Ut viderem poma convallis: ut viderem [Col. 0985D] fructum humillimae in Ecclesia plebis, sicut in Psalmis canitur: Quoniam tu populum humilem salvum facies, et oculos superborum humiliabis (Psal. XVII) .
chunks.english: “I went down to the garden of nuts, to see.” The garden of nuts signifies the canon of the Old and New Testaments. A nut shows one thing in its shell and keeps another thing in its kernel. So if someone does not make this distinction in the holy Scriptures—if, so to speak, he does not look for the inner meaning beneath the nut’s shell—he cannot arrive at the birth of spiritual understanding. And when he says, “to see the fruits of the valley,” he means: to see the fruit of the humblest people in the Church. As is sung in the Book of Psalms, Psalm seventeen: “You will save a humble people, and you will humble the eyes of the proud.”
chunks.notes: The Psalm numbering follows the Latin tradition; in many modern English Bibles this corresponds to Psalm eighteen, verse twenty-seven.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 145. Ut inspicerem si floruissent vineae. Ut probarem si in tantum profecisset Ecclesia ut germinarent in ea qui ad martyrii perfectionem attingerent; et rubicundam, propter Christi sui sanguinis effusionem pulchri essent.
chunks.english: “To see whether the vines had flowered.” That means: to test whether the Church had advanced so far that there would spring up within her people who could reach the perfection of martyrdom—people who would be red and beautiful because of the shedding of the blood of their Christ.
chunks.notes: The printed Latin “et rubicundam ... pulchri essent” does not agree grammatically (feminine singular against masculine plural); the translation renders the evident sense that the martyrs would be red and beautiful through the shedding of the blood of their Christ.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 146. Nescivi, anima mea conturbavit me. Quid nescivit Christus, nisi peccatum? Nescivit etiam illos qui in Evangelio dicunt: Domine, nonne in tuo nomine prophetavimus, et in nomine tuo virtutes multas fecimus? Et tunc (inquit) dicam illis: Amen dico vobis, [Col. 0986A] quia nescio vos (Matth. VII) : non quod eos quales essent nesciret, sed quia nihil boni ex ipsis esset cognovit. Anima mea conturbavit me propter quadrigas Aminadab. Aminadab istum quoque in Christo genealogice reperimus. Unde et has quadrigas in bonam partem accipiendas esse cognoscimus: in quibus evangelistas non incongrue accipimus. Porro autem quod ait. Anima mea conturbavit me, haec conturbatio non est tranquillitati contraria, sed sollicitudini congruens reperitur, secundum illud quod ad Martham in Evangelio dicitur: Quid sollicita es, et turbaris (Luc. X) erga plurima? Et in Psalmis: Commovisti terram, et conturbasti eam, sana contritiones ejus, quia mota est (Psal. LIX) . Unde vero omnes Evangeliorum narrationes narrant nisi per Spiritum [Col. 0986B] sanctum, secundum illud Ezechielis prophetae: Quocunque Spiritus ibat, illuc et rotae pariter ferebantur (Ezech. III et X) .
chunks.english: “I did not know; my soul troubled me.” What did Christ not know, except sin? He also did not know those people who say in the Gospel: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?” Then, he says in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter seven: “I will say to them: Amen, I tell you, I do not know you.” This does not mean that he did not know what kind of people they were. It means that he recognized nothing good in them. “My soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab.” We also find this Amminadab in Christ’s genealogy. Therefore we understand these chariots in a good sense, and it is fitting to take them as the Evangelists. Now when he says, “My soul troubled me,” this disturbance is not opposed to calm; rather, it is found to be in keeping with solicitude. This is like what is said to Martha in the Gospel of Luke, chapter ten: “Why are you anxious and troubled about many things?” And in the Book of Psalms, Psalm fifty-nine: “You shook the earth and troubled it; heal its fractures, for it has been shaken.” And from what source do all the narratives of the Gospels tell their story, if not through the Holy Spirit? This agrees with the prophet Ezekiel, in chapters three and ten, where it says: “Wherever the Spirit went, there the wheels were carried along with it.”
chunks.notes: The Psalm numbering follows the Latin tradition; in many modern English Bibles this is Psalm sixty. The Ezekiel reference in the Latin source gives chapters three and ten; the imagery also closely recalls Ezekiel, chapter one.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 147. Revertere, revertere, Sunamitis. Bis Sunamitem istam in libro Regum laudabili in loco reperimus constitutam: id est, tam illam quae David regi in senectute ministravit, et in ejus complexu virgo quidem pulcherrima permansit (IV Reg. IV) , quam etiam illam cujus Elisaeus filium ex promissione natum et post hoc mortuum suscitavit (III Reg. I) . Quapropter in hoc nomine sanctam Ecclesiam accipiendam esse quis dubitet? Frequenter vero ei revertere dicitur, quae quondam in illo juniore filio in regionem longinquam abiens (Luc. XV) aversa fuerat; tunc etenim reversa est, quando ad Deum ex corde conversa est. [Col. 0986C] Aut idcirco tam crebro ei revertere dicitur, ut etiam si conversa deliquerit, in desperationem non decidat, sed a peccandi consuetudine, spei indulgentia resipiscat. Quae vox ad sanctos utique comprobatur, qui conversae pulchritudinem desiderant intueri.
chunks.english: “Return, return, O Shunammite.” We find this Shunammite twice in the books of Kings, and in both places she is praiseworthy. One is the woman who served King David in his old age and, though held in his embrace, remained a most beautiful virgin, as told in the fourth book of Kings, chapter four. The other is the woman whose son was born by promise and later died, and whom Elisha raised up, as told in the third book of Kings, chapter one. So who could doubt that, under this name, we should understand the holy Church? She is often told, “Return,” because once, in the person of the younger son, she had gone away into a distant country and turned aside, as the Gospel of Luke, chapter fifteen, says. She truly returned when she was converted to God from the heart. Or perhaps she is told so often to return so that, even if she sins after conversion, she will not fall into despair. Instead, by hope in forgiveness, she may come back to her senses and leave behind the habit of sinning. This call clearly belongs to the saints, who long to behold the beauty of the one who has returned.
chunks.notes: The Latin source’s citations to the books of Kings appear confused. The woman who served David is Abishag the Shunammite in First Kings, chapter one; the Shunammite whose son Elisha raised is in Second Kings, chapter four.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: The Church as Spiritual Army and Bride
chunks.latin: CAP. VII.
chunks.english: Chapter 7: The Church as Spiritual Army and Bride

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 148. Quid videbitis in Sunamite,
nisi. Quid in Ecclesia intuendum est, nisi dispositio
eorum qui semper in procinctu tanquam in castris constituti,
contra diabolum dimicare non cessant, idcirco
utique, ne fideles fidem amittant: ne religiosi apostatae
efficiantur elevati, ne misericordes avaritia obdurentur,
ne poenitentes revertantur ad vomitum, ne
virgines integritatis decore careant, ne continentes
castimoniae nitorem amittant? Hi sunt in Ecclesia
chori castrorum jugiter in certamine constituti, et
Deo muniente semper invicti.
chunks.english: What will you see in the Shunammite, if not this? What should be looked for in the Church, if not the ordered ranks of those who are always armed and ready, stationed as if in a camp, and never stop fighting against the devil? They fight so that believers may not lose the faith; so that those vowed to religious life may not grow proud and become apostates; so that the merciful may not be hardened by greed; so that penitents may not return to their vomit; so that virgins may not lose the beauty of integrity; and so that the continent may not lose the brightness of chastity. These are the battle formations of the camp within the Church, always engaged in struggle, and, with God defending them, always unconquered.
chunks.notes: The Latin text appears to omit the expected completion of the Song of Songs phrase, “but the ranks of camps.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 149. Quam pulchri sunt gressus tui! Quam
admirandi profectus in his qui verbum Dei annuntiant
in Ecclesia Christi! sicut Apostolus scriptum
in propheta commemorat: Quam speciosi pedes evangelizantium
bona! Et iterum ipse: Calciati pedes in
praeparatione Evangelii pacis (Rom. X) .
chunks.english: How beautiful are your steps! How wonderful is the progress made by those who proclaim the word of God in the Church of Christ. As the Apostle recalls what is written in the prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim good news.” And again he says, in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter ten: “Have your feet shod with readiness for the Gospel of peace.”
chunks.notes: The first quotation is from Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter ten, verse fifteen. The second is from Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter six, verse fifteen, though the printed Latin cites Romans chapter ten.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 150. Junctura femorum tuorum. Juncturam femorum
tuorum, ex circumcisione et praeputio venientium
societatem advertimus populorum; et per id,
tam illi qui ex femore Abraham secundum carnem
propagati sunt, quam illi qui in semine ejus, id est
in Christo, meruerunt; cum in unitatem fidei copulantur,
tanquam monilia quae fabricata sunt manu
artificis, describuntur. Quis enim artifex tanquam
monilia, hos in fide populos sociavit, nisi ille de quo
Apostolus ait: Ipse est pax nostra, qui fecit utraque
unum (Ephes. VI) ?
chunks.english: “The joints of your thighs.” By the joining of your thighs we understand the fellowship of peoples who come both from circumcision and from uncircumcision. That is, those who were born according to the flesh from the thigh of Abraham, and those who were counted worthy in Abraham’s seed, that is, in Christ, are joined together in the unity of faith. So they are described as ornaments fashioned by the hand of a craftsman. And who is the craftsman who joined these peoples in faith like ornaments, if not the one of whom the Apostle says, in Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter six: “He is our peace, who made both peoples one”?
chunks.notes: The quotation is from Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two, verse fourteen; the printed Latin gives Ephesians chapter six.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 151. Umbilicus tuus crater tornatilis. Hi qui
non extremo, sed in medio Ecclesiae corpore commutantur,
umbiculus dicuntur. Crater tornatilis vasa
sunt utilia in eo tornatilia, quia ad obediendum vel
ad omne opus bonum parata (Ephes. II) , nunquam
indigent poculis quia Spiritus sancti gratia semper
repleta sunt.
chunks.english: “Your navel is a turned bowl.” Those who are changed, not at the far edges, but in the middle of the Church’s body, are called the navel. The turned bowl represents useful vessels—turned and shaped because they are ready to obey and prepared for every good work, as Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two, says. They never lack drink, because they are always filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit.
chunks.notes: The phrase “prepared for every good work” echoes the second letter to Timothy, chapter two, verse twenty-one, though the printed text cites Paul’s letter to the Ephesians, chapter two.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 152. Venter tuus sicut acervus tritici. Qui semper
sancta Scripturarum alimenta percipiunt, et ea
quae sunt salutaria infra se congerunt, in ventris similitudine
deputantur, et hi velut acervus tritici
congestus merito pronuntiantur, quia ex doctrina
sana ex qua quotidie replentur, multos affatim reficiunt;
quae doctrina in tantum proficit, ut etiam ad
virginitatis observantiam piis persuasionibus multos
adducat.
chunks.english: “Your belly is like a heap of wheat.” Those who are always receiving the holy nourishment of the Scriptures, and who store up within themselves what leads to salvation, are compared to the belly. They are rightly called a piled-up heap of wheat, because from the sound teaching with which they are filled each day, they refresh many people in abundance. This teaching is so fruitful that, by devout persuasion, it even leads many to preserve virginity.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 153. Duo ubera sicut duo hinnuli. Duo testamenta
duobus hinnulis capreae, id est ex peccati traduce
venientibus populis coaptata. Ex his enim operibus
nutriuntur, qui originali peccato obnoxii, in
Christo tanquam hinnuli renascuntur.
chunks.english: “Your two breasts are like two young fawns.” The two Testaments are fitted to two young fawns of a doe—that is, to the peoples who come from the stock of sin. For those who are subject to original sin are nourished by these works, and in Christ they are reborn like young fawns.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 154. Collum tuum sicut turris eburnea. Notitia
Scripturarum, quae frequenti in meditatione conquiritur,
velut turris eburnea, in colli pulchritudine
designatur. Idcirco autem turris eburnea, quia qui
verbo Dei assistunt, quotidiano profectu per nitorem
justitiae in excelsiora proficiunt.
chunks.english: “Your neck is like an ivory tower.” Knowledge of the Scriptures, gained through constant meditation, is indicated by the beauty of the neck, like an ivory tower. It is called an ivory tower because those who serve the word of God, through daily growth and through the brightness of righteousness, advance to higher things.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 155. Oculi tui sicut piscinae in Esebon. Spirituales
doctores tui constituti in porta, in Christo sicut
aquae irriguae ad erudiendos populos. Idcirco
namque piscinae, quia Spiritus sancti repleti sunt
scientia. In alio libro etiam ipse Salomon dicit: Exstruxi
piscinas aquarum, ut irrigarem silvas lignorum
germinantium (Eccle. II) .
chunks.english: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon.” Your spiritual teachers, stationed at the gate, are in Christ like irrigating waters for the instruction of the peoples. They are called pools because they are filled with the knowledge of the Holy Spirit. Solomon himself says in another book, in Ecclesiastes, chapter two: “I built pools of water for myself, so that I might water a forest of growing trees.”
chunks.notes: The quotation is from Ecclesiastes, chapter two, verse six.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 156. Nasus tuus sicut turris Libani. Nasus Ecclesiae
illi sunt qui odorem justitiae qui est in Christo,
percipientes, ad cordis interna trajiciunt. Hi
qui in magna virtute consistunt, sicut turris Libani
disponuntur. Libanum autem candorem esse jam
superius diximus: horum proceritatis candor respicit
contra Damascum, quia sapientia eorum, quae ex
Deo est, illuminat mundum.
chunks.english: “Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon.” The nose of the Church means those who perceive the fragrance of righteousness that is in Christ, and carry it into the inner places of the heart. These people, who stand firm in great virtue, are arranged like the tower of Lebanon. As mentioned earlier, Lebanon means whiteness. The bright height of these people faces toward Damascus, because their wisdom, which comes from God, enlightens the world.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 157. Caput tuum ut Carmelus, et comae. In
Carmelo monte, sancti Elias et Elisaeus saepe receptaculum
habuere (III Reg. XVIII) : quapropter in
capite Ecclesiae Domino nostro Jesu Christo, quo sublimius
ut est (tanquam in monte Carmelo) et justi
habitaculum, et multitudo populorum tanquam diversitas
animalium sapientiae percipiunt alimentum.
Comae capitis istius, sicut purpura regis juncta canalibus:
eminentiores quippe sancti, beati videlicet martyres
Christi, consimilati per purpuram regalibus ornamentis,
et salutaribus semper copulati intelliguntur
doctrinis.
chunks.english: “Your head is like Carmel, and your hair.” On Mount Carmel, the holy prophets Elijah and Elisha often had a place of refuge, as the third book of Kings, chapter eighteen, records. Therefore, in the head of the Church, our Lord Jesus Christ, who is most exalted—as on Mount Carmel—both the righteous find a dwelling place, and the multitude of peoples, like many kinds of living creatures, receive the food of wisdom. The hair of this head is like royal purple fastened to channels. That is, the more eminent saints, especially the blessed martyrs of Christ, are compared through the image of purple to royal ornaments, and are understood as always joined to teachings that bring salvation.
chunks.notes: The Latin cites the third book of Kings, chapter eighteen, according to the Vulgate numbering; in many modern Bibles this corresponds to the first book of Kings, chapter eighteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 158. Statura tua assimilata est palmae. Perfectio
tua pervenit ad praemium, et doctores tui dulces
effecti sunt per Spiritum sanctum.
chunks.english: “Your stature is like a palm tree.” Your perfection has reached its reward, and your teachers have been made sweet through the Holy Spirit.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 159. Dixi, ascendam in palmam. Illi in palmam
ascendunt qui in Christi cruce proficiunt, de
quibus Apostolus dicit: qui in Christo sunt, carnem
suam crucifixerunt cum vitiis et concupiscentiis. Ipsi autem
fructus hujus palmae (sanctae crucis) praemia
consequuntur, qui illud, si tamen compatimur ut et
glorificemur (Rom. VIII) , cum eodem Apostolo dicunt.
chunks.english: “I said: I will climb the palm tree.” Those climb the palm tree who make progress in the cross of Christ. Of them the Apostle says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” And those receive the fruits of this palm tree—the rewards of the holy cross—who say with the same Apostle, in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight: “If we suffer with him, we shall also be glorified with him.”
chunks.notes: The first Pauline quotation is from Paul’s letter to the Galatians, chapter five, verse twenty-four. The second is from Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight, verse seventeen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 160. Et erunt ubera tua sicut botri vineae. Nec
etenim alii reperiuntur, qui nascentes in fide enutriant,
nisi doctores Ecclesiae.
chunks.english: “And your breasts will be like clusters of the vine.” For no others are found to nourish those being born in the faith except the teachers of the Church.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 161. Et odores tui sicut malorum. Et suavitas
eruditionis tuae per eos propagabitur, qui sobrie
et juste vivendo odorem bonae conversationis propinare
non desinunt.
chunks.english: “And your fragrance will be like apples.” The sweetness of your instruction will be spread through those who live soberly and justly, and who never stop offering the fragrance of a good way of life.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 162. Guttur tuum sicut vinum optimum. Possunt
etiam in gutture illi sancti intelligi per quos lex
et prophetae et evangelica doctrina pronuntiata est:
quae utique sancta Scriptura eximio sapore praedita,
ut vinum optimum redolet ac resplendet, et per Spiritum
sanctum potantes inebriat.
chunks.english: “Your throat is like the finest wine.” The throat can also be understood as those holy people through whom the Law, the Prophets, and the teaching of the Gospel were proclaimed. This holy Scripture, endowed with an excellent taste, gives off fragrance and shines like the finest wine, and through the Holy Spirit it makes those who drink it spiritually intoxicated.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 163. Dignum dilecto meo potandum. De sacra
Scriptura Christi potant, cum ex ea Christiani, qui
sunt membra ipsius, miris modis et incomparabili
dulcedine satiantur.
chunks.english: “Worthy for my beloved to drink.” Christians drink from the sacred Scripture of Christ when, from it, they—the members of his body—are satisfied in marvelous ways and with incomparable sweetness.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 164. Labiisque et dentibus illius ad rummandum.
Labia et dentes Christi doctores Ecclesiae:
hi quod sanctum est ruminare non desinunt, cum ea
quae ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt, quotidie
meditantur.
chunks.english: “And for his lips and teeth to chew over.” The lips and teeth of Christ are the teachers of the Church. They never stop chewing over what is holy, because they meditate every day on the things written for our instruction.
chunks.notes: The Latin verb is printed as “rummandum,” apparently for “ruminandum,” meaning to chew over or meditate on.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 165. Ego dilecto meo, et ad me conversio ejus.
Huic dilecto, ex voce Ecclesiae dicitur: adhaesit
anima mea post te, me suscepit dextera (Psal. LXII) . Videamus
et alibi quomodo ipsa dilecto suo loquatur:
Nos autem populus tuus, et oves gregis tui (Psal.
LXXVIII) . Et quomodo ad me conversio ejus, dicit propheta:
Eritque antequam clament, ego exaudiam, adhuc
illis loquentibus ego exaudiam (Isai. LXVI) , dicit
Dominus. Sed nulla est ad Ecclesiam tam evidens
Christi conversio, nisi cum Verbum caro factum est,
et habitavit in nobis (Joan. I) .
chunks.english: “I belong to my beloved, and his turning is toward me.” To this beloved, speaking in the voice of the Church, it is said in Psalm sixty-two: “My soul clung after you; your right hand upheld me.” Let us also see elsewhere how the Church speaks to her beloved, in Psalm seventy-eight: “But we are your people, and the sheep of your flock.” And how is his turning toward me? The prophet says, in Isaiah, chapter sixty-six: “Before they call, I will answer; while they are still speaking, I will hear, says the Lord.” But there is no turning of Christ toward the Church more evident than this, in the Gospel of John, chapter one: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
chunks.notes: The cited passages are from the Psalms, psalm sixty-two, verse nine in the Vulgate; the Psalms, psalm seventy-eight, verse thirteen in the Vulgate; Isaiah, chapter sixty-five, verse twenty-four, though the printed Latin gives Isaiah chapter sixty-six; and the Gospel of John, chapter one, verse fourteen.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 166. Veni, dilecte mi, egrediamur. Egreditur
Christus cum Ecclesia in agro, quando cum sanctis
praedictis visitat mundum, sicut in Evangelio scriptum
est: Qui seminat bonum semen, est filius hominis
(Matth. XIII; Marc. XIV) ; ager est mundus. Commoremur
in villis; in populis credentibus circumquaque
diffusis, in quibus Christus per fidem habitat; non
sine Ecclesia, cum eosdem ipsos in suis membris
reputans, suam efficit Ecclesiam.
chunks.english: “Come, my beloved, let us go out.” Christ goes out with the Church into the field when, together with the saints already mentioned, he visits the world. As it is written in the Gospel, in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter thirteen, and the Gospel of Mark, chapter fourteen: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man,” and, “the field is the world.” “Let us stay in the villages”—that is, among the believing peoples spread everywhere. Christ dwells in them through faith, not apart from the Church, because he counts these very people among his own members and makes them his Church.
chunks.notes: The Gospel quotation is from the Gospel of Matthew, chapter thirteen, verses thirty-seven through thirty-eight. The printed Latin also cites the Gospel of Mark, chapter fourteen, but the wording belongs to Matthew.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 167. Mane surgamus ad vineas. Ut animae
quae per fidem coli jam meruerunt, in matutinis Christum
resurrexisse cognoscant, ne ultra de sui corporis
resurrectione diffidant.
chunks.english: “Let us rise early and go to the vineyards.” This means that souls already made worthy to be cultivated through faith should recognize, in the morning light, that Christ has risen, so that they may no longer doubt the resurrection of their own body.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 168. Videamus si floruit vinea. Appareat, si
fideles, quae corde crediderunt ore pronuntient, sicut
Apostolus ait: Corde creditur ad justitiam, ore autem
confessio fit ad salutem (Rom. X) ; vel si flores fructus
parturiunt, si in eis per sancta desideria pietatis
opera prodierunt.
chunks.english: “Let us see whether the vineyard has blossomed.” Let it become clear whether the faithful proclaim with their mouth what they have believed in their heart. As the Apostle says, in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter ten: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Or, let it become clear whether the blossoms are giving birth to fruit—that is, whether works of devotion have come forth in them through holy desires.
chunks.notes: The quotation is from Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter ten, verse ten.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 169. Si floruerunt mata punica. Si illi qui in
Christo crediderunt in tanta dilectione proficiunt ut
etiam occidi pro ipso omnibus modis delectentur.
Vis videre malum punicum, audi in Actibus apostolorum
Paulum apostolum: Ego, inquit, non solum
judicari in Jerusalem, sed et mori pro Christo paratus
sum (Act. XXI) .
chunks.english: “Whether the pomegranates have blossomed.” This asks whether those who have believed in Christ are advancing in such great love that they are even glad, in every way, to be killed for his sake. Do you want to see a pomegranate? Listen to the apostle Paul in the Acts of the Apostles. He says: “I am ready not only to be judged in Jerusalem, but also to die for Christ.”
chunks.notes: The quotation is from the Acts of the Apostles, chapter twenty-one, verse thirteen. The printed Latin has “mata punica,” apparently for “mala punica,” pomegranates.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 170. Ibi dabo tibi ubera tua. In hac sancta
confessione sociabuntur tibi doctores mei, comparati
ut patiantur pro te, qui quoque sine fine regnabunt
apud te.
chunks.english: “There I will give you your breasts.” In this holy confession my teachers will be joined to you, prepared to suffer for you; and they too will reign with you without end.
chunks.notes: The printed lemma reads “ubera tua” where the Vulgate has “ubera mea”; the translation follows the printed text, which the exposition (“my teachers will be joined to you”) presupposes.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 171. Mandragorae dederunt odorem. Hi qui alta
radice fide fundati sunt, et quadam disciplinae vel
parcimoniae austeritate vigere noscuntur, publicis
praedicationibus populos instruxerunt, odorem suavitatis
ex conversatione sanctissima propinantes.
chunks.english: “The mandrakes have given their fragrance.” Those who are founded in faith with a deep root, and who are known to flourish through a certain austerity of discipline and self-restraint, have instructed the peoples through public preaching, offering the sweet fragrance that comes from a most holy way of life.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 172. Omnia dona nova et vetera. Quoniam
tam in patriarchis et prophetis quam in apostolis et
martyribus ego ipse nova et vetera servavi tibi; quia
illi te pronuntiaverunt et crediderunt venturum, isti
praedicare non desinunt ex Virgine natum ac pro salute
omnium passum, et post resurrectionem in coelos
assumptum.
chunks.english: “All gifts, new and old.” For in the patriarchs and prophets, and also in the apostles and martyrs, I myself have kept new and old gifts for you. The former proclaimed you and believed that you would come; the latter never cease to preach that you were born of the Virgin, suffered for the salvation of all, and, after the resurrection, were taken up into heaven.

chunks.speaker: announcer
chunks.chapter_title: The Church Is Sealed by Christ’s Love
chunks.latin: CAP. VIII.
chunks.english: Chapter eight: The Church Is Sealed by Christ’s Love

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 173. Quis mihi det te fratrem meum. Sugit ubera matris Christus cum mysteriis priscae legis reficitur Christianus populus, vel cum spiritualibus sacramentis doctores et piissima expositione, tanquam vero lacte reficiunt.
chunks.english: “Who will give you to me as my brother?” Christ suckles at his mother’s breasts when the Christian people are refreshed by the mysteries of the ancient Law, or when teachers nourish them with spiritual sacraments and with a most devout interpretation, as though feeding them with true milk.
chunks.notes: The Latin likely reflects the Song of Songs phrase about the beloved nursing at the mother’s breasts.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 174. Ut inveniam te foras et osculer. Ut te, inquit, quem Veteris Testamenti figurae tegebant, per Evangelium, ego in veritate reperiam. Et bene ait: Te foris inveniam, quia illi juniori filio de regione longinqua redeunti, pater in occursum regressus est (Luc. XV): ut deosculer te, inquit, ut tibi reconciliari merear; et jam nemo me despiciet; videlicet ut non dicatur Petro, pro Cornelio quem gratia Spiritus sancti praevenerat: Quare introisti ad viros praeputium habentes, et manducasti cum illis? Sed ipse Petrus pronuntiet: In veritate comperio, quoniam personarum acceptio non est apud Deum, sed in omni loco, et in omni gente, qui timet eum et operatur justitiam, acceptus est illi (Act. XI).
chunks.english: “So that I may find you outside and kiss you.” She is saying: “You, whom the figures of the Old Testament kept hidden, I will now truly find through the Gospel.” And she rightly says, “I will find you outside,” because when the younger son returned from a far country, the father came out to meet him, as the Gospel of Luke says in chapter fifteen. “Then I may kiss you,” she says, “and be found worthy to be reconciled to you; and then no one will despise me.” In other words, no one will say to Peter, on account of Cornelius, whom the grace of the Holy Spirit had gone before: “Why did you go in to men who are uncircumcised and eat with them?” Instead, Peter himself will declare, as the Acts of the Apostles says in chapter eleven: “In truth I have discovered that God shows no partiality. In every place and in every nation, whoever fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 175. Apprehendam te, et ducam te. Cum enim te apprehendero tibique per fidem adhaesero, restat ut introducam te in domum matris meae: in congregationem videlicet Jerusalem: illuc utique te introducam, quando cum omnibus bonis quae per tuam gratiam consecuta sum etiam ipsa perduci eo, hoc est ad coelestem Hierosolymam, meruero.
chunks.english: “I will take hold of you and lead you.” Once I have taken hold of you and clung to you by faith, it remains for me to bring you into my mother’s house, that is, into the assembly of Jerusalem. I will surely bring you there when, together with all the good things I have received through your grace, I myself am found worthy to be brought there also—that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 176. Ibi me docebis, et dabo tibi poculum. Ibi me docebis, ut jam non in aenigmate per speculum, sed facie ad faciem videam; et non ex parte sicut nunc, sed tunc cognoscam sicut et cognitus sum (I Cor. XIII), ut ille ait: Et dabo tibi poculum ex vino condito, et mustum malogranatorum: quando optimos et dulcissimos protulero martyrum sanctorum fructus, et filii hominum qui in umbra alarum tuarum sperant, inebriabuntur a pinguedine domus tuae, et torrente deliciarum tuarum potabis eos (Psal. XXXV).
chunks.english: “There you will teach me, and I will give you a cup.” There you will teach me, so that I may no longer see in a riddle, as in a mirror, but face to face; and so that I may no longer know only in part, as I do now, but then know as I have also been known, as Paul says in his first letter to the Corinthians, chapter thirteen. “And I will give you a cup from spiced wine, and the new wine of pomegranates,” when I have brought forth the finest and sweetest fruits of the holy martyrs. Then, as Psalm thirty-five says, “The children of men, who hope in the shadow of your wings, will be filled with the richness of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delights.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 177. Laeva ejus sub capite meo, et dextera illius amplexabitur me. Adjuro vos, filiae Jerusalem. Haec quae in hoc loco scripta sunt, in superioribus jam praedicta, et Christo illuminante reperiuntur exposita. Sed idcirco arbitror iterato in hoc libro conscripta, ut vehementius cordi insideant; et bis insinuata vivaciori memoria renoventur. Haec jubent spernenda temporalia; et infra nos posita, velut sinistram sub capite constitutam edocent; et coelestem gloriam quae nos ex superiori parte, tanquam dextera complexatur, exspectandam admonent; vel illud, ut servituri Domino, voluntarii non inviti quae sunt sancta perficiant, secundum quod Petrus apostolus docet: Pascite qui in vobis est gregem Dei, non coacti sed spontanei (I Petr. V).
chunks.english: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem.” These words written here have already been stated earlier and, with Christ’s illumination, have already been explained. But I think they were written a second time in this book so that they might sink more deeply into the heart, and, by being repeated, be renewed in a more living memory. They teach us that temporal things must be despised and placed beneath us, like the left hand set under the head. They also remind us to wait for the heavenly glory that embraces us from above, like the right hand. Or else they teach this: that those who are going to serve the Lord should carry out holy duties willingly, not reluctantly, in keeping with what the apostle Peter teaches in his first letter, chapter five: “Shepherd the flock of God that is among you, not under compulsion, but willingly.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 178. Quae est ista quae ascendit de deserto? Bene de deserto ascendere describitur, cui propheta dicit: Pro eo quod fuisti derelicta et odio habita, et non erat qui pertransiret (Isai. LX), etc. De cujus etiam filiis in Psalmis canitur: Erraverunt in solitudine, in siccitate, viam civitatis habitationis non invenerunt. Esurientes et sitientes, anima eorum in idipsis defecit, et clamaverunt ad Dominum cum tribularentur, et de necessitatibus eorum liberavit eos; deduxit eos per viam rectam ut irent in civitatem habitationis (Psal. X). Idcirco sequitur.
chunks.english: “Who is this who comes up from the desert?” She is rightly described as coming up from the desert, for the prophet says to her in Isaiah, chapter sixty: “Because you were abandoned and hated, and there was no one passing through you,” and so on. Of her children, too, the Psalms sing, in Psalm ten: “They wandered in the wilderness, in a dry place; they did not find the way to a city where they could dwell. Hungry and thirsty, their soul failed within them. Then they cried to the Lord in their trouble, and he delivered them from their necessities. He led them by the right way, so that they might go to a city where they could dwell.” Therefore the text continues.
chunks.notes: The printed citation “Psalm ten” appears to be erroneous; the quoted passage corresponds to Psalm one hundred six in the Vulgate numbering, Psalm one hundred seven in many English Bibles.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 179. Deliciis affluens. Unde et populus Israel e deserto egrediens, in terram promissionis lacte et melle fluentem ingreditur; et ille filius qui de siliquis porcorum pasci cupiens saturari non poterat, ad convivium quod de pingui occiso vitulo pater praeparavit reficiendus inducitur. Has delicias a deserto veniens Ecclesia, in Christo multiplices reperit; et nixa super dilectum scribitur, quia ad ipsam per prophetam idem dilectus dicti: Ego feci, ego feram, ego portabo, et ego salvabo (Isai. XLVI).
chunks.english: “Overflowing with delights.” For this reason, when the people of Israel came out of the desert, they entered the promised land, flowing with milk and honey. And the son who longed to feed on the pods of swine but could not be satisfied was brought in to be refreshed at the banquet prepared by his father from the fattened calf that had been killed. Coming from the desert, the Church finds these delights in many forms in Christ. And she is described as leaning upon her beloved, because that same beloved says to her through the prophet, in Isaiah, chapter forty-six: “I have made; I will carry; I will bear; and I will save.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 180. Sub arbore mali suscitavi vos. In odorifero crucis patibulo ubi ego occubui, illic te a peccatorum interitu suscitavi, quando te credentem signo crucis praenotare praecipio.
chunks.english: “Under the apple tree I awakened you.” On the fragrant wood of the cross, where I lay down in death, there I raised you from the destruction of sins, when I command that you, as a believer, be marked beforehand with the sign of the cross.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 181. Ibi corrupta est mater tua. Ubi tu per meam mortem suscitari meruisti, illic per suam impietatem Synagoga capta est quando Crucifige clamabat; et, Sanguis hujus super nos et super filios nostros (Luc. XXIII), Pilato judicante respondit.
chunks.english: “There your mother was corrupted.” In the very place where you were found worthy to be raised up through my death, there the Synagogue was trapped by her own ungodliness, when she cried out, “Crucify him,” and, as Pilate sat in judgment, answered, as the Gospel of Luke, chapter twenty-three, relates, “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”
chunks.notes: The Latin cites the Gospel of Luke, chapter twenty-three, but the wording “His blood be upon us and upon our children” is from the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-seven, verse twenty-five.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 182. Pone me ut signaculum. Ita ut cum Psalmista dicere possis, Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine, dedisti laetitiam in corde meo (Psal. IV). Quoniam quaecunque signata sunt facile temerari non possunt, sic recipe fidem meam, ut eam integram illibatamque custodias, et quem per crucis signaculum accepisti thesaurum justitiae quem in te contuli, a nullo fore contingendum ullo modo pertimescas.
chunks.english: “Set me as a seal.” Then you will be able to say with the psalmist, in Psalm four: “The light of your face, Lord, has been sealed upon us; you have given joy in my heart.” Since things that have been sealed cannot easily be violated, receive my faith in such a way that you guard it whole and undefiled. And do not in any way fear that anyone can touch the treasure of righteousness that you received through the seal of the cross—the treasure I have placed within you.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 183. Ut signaculum pone me. Primitus super cor, inde super brachium signaculum superponendum intellige: id est, ut tam in cogitatione quam in opere, ad meum signum accurras; ac te, per hoc, non alterius, sed mei esse demonstres; meque contutante, integra perseveres.
chunks.english: “Set me as a seal.” Understand that the seal is to be placed first upon the heart, and then upon the arm. That means: in both thought and action, run to my sign, and by this show that you belong not to another, but to me. Then, with me watching over you, you will persevere unharmed.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 184. Quia fortis ut mors dilectio tua. In tantum dilexi te, ut mori voluerim prote; et haec erat fortitudo amoris, acerbitas mortis. Dura autem sicut infernus aemulatio; ut sancti quoque econtrario pro Christo occidi non metuant, quem pro sua salute mortem suscepisse sine dubio cognoverunt.
chunks.english: “For your love is strong as death.” I loved you so much that I was willing to die for you; and this was the strength of love: the bitterness of death. “Jealousy is hard as hell,” so that, in return, the saints do not fear being killed for Christ, since they know without doubt that he accepted death for their salvation.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 185. Lampades ejus, lampades ignis. Vasa in quibus castistas habitat, semper sunt splendida et Spiritus sancti igne ferventia.
chunks.english: “Its lamps are lamps of fire.” The vessels in which chastity dwells are always shining and burning with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 186. Aquae multae non potuerunt exstinguere charitatem, nec flumina obruent illam, nec tribulationes; nullae quamlibet validae persecutiones dilectionem quae est ex Deo, vel circa Deum, perturbare vel vincere possunt, secundum illud quod Apostolus dicit: Quis nos separabit a charitate Christi? an tribulatio, an angustia, an persecutio, an fames, an nuditas, an gladius, an periculum? certus sum enim quia neque mors, neque vita, neque angeli, neque principatus, neque excelsum, neque profundum, neque creatura alia poterit nos separare a charitate Dei, quae est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro (Rom. VIII).
chunks.english: “Many waters could not extinguish love, nor will rivers overwhelm it.” No troubles, no persecutions, however powerful, can disturb or overcome the love that comes from God and is directed toward God. This agrees with what the Apostle says in Paul’s letter to the Romans, chapter eight: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will trouble, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or the sword, or danger? For I am certain that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 187. Si dederit homo omnem substantiam. Tanquam dicat: Et si distribuero in cibos pauperum omnes facultates meas, et si tradidero corpus meum ut ardeam, charitatem autem non habeam, nihil mihi prodest (I Cor. XIII). Hac enim nihil pretiosius, ut Joannes apostolus ait: Quia Deus charitas est; et qui manet in charitate in Deo manet.
chunks.english: “If a person should give away all his possessions.” It is as if Scripture were saying, in the words of Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter thirteen: “Even if I distribute all my goods as food for the poor, and even if I hand over my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.” For nothing is more precious than love, as the apostle John says: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 188. Soror nostra parva, et ubera non habet. Ecclesia ex gentibus veniens, rudis adhuc ad credendum, et nec dum praedita viris eruditis ad docendum, secundum quod Apostolus loquitur: Non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed tanquam parvulis in Christo lac vobis potum dedi, non escam; nondum enim poteratis, sed nec quidem adhuc potestis, adhuc enim estis carnales (I Cor. III). Et alibi: Saecularia judicia si habueritis, contemptibiles qui sunt in Ecclesia, illos constituite ad judicandum. Ad verecundiam vestram dico: si non est inter vos sapiens quisquam qui possit judicare inter fratrem suum (I Cor. VI)? Dum eos in tanta pusillanimitate redarguit, utique adhuc pusillam in fide, et necdum spiritualibus nutrimentis habilem plebem ostendit.
chunks.english: “Our sister is little, and she has no breasts.” This refers to the Church coming from the Gentiles: still inexperienced in believing, and not yet supplied with learned men capable of teaching. It is like what the Apostle says in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter three: “I could not speak to you as to spiritual people, but as to little children in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to take it. Indeed, even now you still cannot, for you are still fleshly.” And elsewhere, in Paul’s first letter to the Corinthians, chapter six, he says: “If you have disputes about worldly matters, appoint as judges those who are least esteemed in the Church. I say this to your shame: is there no one wise among you who can judge between brothers?” By rebuking them for such smallness, he clearly shows that this people is still little in faith and not yet ready for spiritual nourishment.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 189. Quid faciemus sorori nostrae? Quemadmodum disponemus Ecclesiam tempore quo ad fidem vocanda est?
chunks.english: “What shall we do for our sister?” That is: how shall we arrange the Church at the time when she is to be called to faith?

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 190. Si murus est, aedificemus super eum. Qui coeperunt in fide crescere et ita stabiliri ut robore suo infirmos quosque commoneant; suscepto honoris privilegio, ad caeteros docendos instituantur, secundum quod Paulus ad Timotheum: Haec commenda fidelibus qui idonei erunt et alios docere (II Tim. II). Et iterum ad Titum: Hujus rei gratia reliqui te Cretae, ut ea quae desunt corrigas, et constituas per civitates presbyteros, sicut ego tibi disposui. Dum ista sic in Ecclesia disponuntur, tanquam propugnacula argentea muris adjiciuntur.
chunks.english: “If she is a wall, let us build upon it.” Those who have begun to grow in faith and become so firm that by their own strength they can encourage the weak should, after receiving the privilege of office, be appointed to teach the rest. As Paul says to Timothy in his second letter, chapter two: “Entrust these things to faithful people who will be capable of teaching others also.” And again Paul says to Titus, chapter one: “For this reason I left you in Crete: that you should correct what is lacking and appoint presbyters in each city, as I directed you.” When these things are arranged in this way in the Church, it is as though silver battlements are added to the walls.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 191. Si ostium est, compingamus. Dicit Propheta in Psalmis: Pone, Domine, custodiam ori meo, et ostium circumstantiae labiis meis (Psal. CXL). Itaque si est quis idoneus ad loquendum, et velut ostium quod aperitur et clauditur, tempus loquendi vel tacendi intelligit; hoc tale ostium tabulis cedrinis compingamus, ut dum odoriferum lignum in se suscepit, cum Paulo dicere possit: Mihi absit gloriari nisi in cruce Domini nostri Jesu Christi, per quem mihi mundus crucifixus est, et ego mundo (Gal. VI).
chunks.english: “If she is a door, let us fasten it together.” The prophet says in Psalm one hundred forty: “Set a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.” So, if someone is fit for speaking, and, like a door that is opened and closed, understands the proper time to speak and the proper time to be silent, let us fasten such a door with cedar boards. Then, once he has received fragrant wood within himself, he can say with Paul, in his letter to the Galatians, chapter six: “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 192. Ego murus et ubera mea sicut turris. Vox Ecclesiae est, tam in fide quam pro fide proficientis: Ego murus; quia ipse aedificavit me qui fortissimus pugnat pro me. Et ubera mea sicut turris. Construente Deo, proceritate justitiae creverunt, et in me parvulos qui in Christo sunt, nutriunt; et donec ad perfectionis cibum perveniant, eos educare non desinunt, quoadusque eis voce sapientiae dicatur: Relinquite infantiam, et venite ambulare per vias prudentiae.
chunks.english: “I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower.” This is the voice of the Church as she advances both in faith and on behalf of the faith. “I am a wall,” because the one who built me fights for me with supreme strength. “And my breasts are like a tower.” Built up by God, they have grown tall through righteousness. In me, they nourish the little ones who are in Christ, and they do not stop raising them until they reach the food of maturity—until the voice of Wisdom says to them: “Leave childhood behind, and come walk in the ways of prudence.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin: Num. 193. Ex quo facta sum coram eo. Ex quo Christo pacem reperi, ex eo et murorum praesidia et turrium propugnacula cum decore suscepi, cum eis ab eo qui me condidit civitas esse promerui, habens munimenta in sanctis, et decorem retinens in electis.
chunks.english: “From the time I became so before him.” From the time I found peace in Christ, from that time I received, with beauty, the protection of walls and the defenses of towers. Along with them, I was found worthy to be a city established by the one who created me: having fortifications in the saints, and preserving beauty in the elect.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 194. Vinea fuit pacifico. Cultura assidua ad
[Col. 0992C] hibita est a Christo in Ecclesia quae illos habet populos
de quibus in Psalmis canitur: Plantati in domo
Domini, in atriis Dei nostri florebunt (Psal. XCI) . Tradidit
eam custodibus. Commisit eam regendam apostolis
vel successoribus eorum episcopis. Ad quam, sub nomine
Jerusalem, dicit Dominus per prophetam: Super
te et super muros tuos posui custodes tuos, tota die et
nocte, usque in finem contacebunt (Isai. VIII) .
chunks.english: “The vineyard belonged to the Peaceful One.” This means that Christ has continually cultivated the Church, the Church that contains those peoples of whom the Psalm says: “Planted in the house of the Lord, they will flourish in the courts of our God,” in Psalm ninety-one. “He entrusted it to keepers.” That is, he committed it to the apostles to govern, or to their successors, the bishops. Under the name of Jerusalem, the Lord says to this Church through the prophet: “Upon you and upon your walls I have appointed your watchmen; all day and all night, until the end, they will not be silent,” in the book of Isaiah, chapter eight.
chunks.notes: The printed citation “Psalm ninety-one” follows the Latin numbering. The Isaiah citation is printed as chapter eight, but the quotation corresponds to Isaiah chapter sixty-two, verse six. The Latin reading “contacebunt” appears corrupt; the sense required is “they will not be silent.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 195. Vir affert fructus ejus mille argenteos.
Christus de quo propheta dicit: Ecce vir, Oriens nomen
ejus (Zach. VI) . Compensat regnum coelorum pro
sanctis laboribus vel eleemosynis, secundum illud
quod in Evangelio dicitur: Venite, benedicti Patris
mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab origine
mundi, quia esurivi, et dedistis mihi manducare,
[Col. 0992D] sitivi, et dedistis mihi bibere; hospes fui, et collegistis
me; nudus, et operuistis me; infirmus et in carcere, et
venistis ad me (Matth. XXV) . In mille autem argenteis
plenitudo totius remunerationis ostenditur, et merces
consummata justorum.
chunks.english: “The man brings a thousand silver pieces for its fruit.” This man is Christ, of whom the prophet says: “Behold the man; his name is the Rising One,” in the book of Zechariah, chapter six. Christ gives the kingdom of heaven in return for holy labors and works of mercy, according to what is said in the Gospel: “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me; I was naked, and you clothed me; I was sick and in prison, and you came to me,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-five. And in the thousand silver pieces, the fullness of the whole reward is shown: the completed recompense of the righteous.
chunks.notes: “The Rising One” translates Oriens, a messianic title often rendered “Branch” or “Dayspring.”

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 196. Vinea mea coram me est. Secundum
quod in Psalmis canitur: Oculi Domini super justos,
et aures ejus in preces eorum. Dicit enim Apostolus
Quoniam ipse Dominus in jussu et in voce archangeli
et in tuba Dei descendet de coelo, et mortui qui in Christo
sunt resurgent primi, deinde nos qui vivimus, qui relinquimur,
simul rapiemur cum illis obviam Domino in
aera, et sic semper cum Domino erimus (I Thess. IV) .
Igitur quia semper post resurrectionem sancti cum
[Col. 0993A] Domino sunt, idcirco Dominus dicit, Vinea mea coram
me est.
chunks.english: “My vineyard is before me.” This agrees with what is sung in the Psalms: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers.” For the Apostle says: “The Lord himself, with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord,” in Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians, chapter four. Therefore, because after the resurrection the saints are always with the Lord, the Lord says, “My vineyard is before me.”
chunks.notes: The psalm quotation echoes Psalm thirty-three in the Latin numbering, Psalm thirty-four in many English Bibles.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 197. Mille tui pacifici et ducenti his. Duodecim
quippe si per centenum numerum amplientur,
mille ducentos efficiunt; qui numerus utique apostolicis
viris, qui ex eis spiritualiter per Evangelium
in Christo sunt geniti, convenit, qui in summa perfectione
constituti, tanquam illa terra optima, per
centesimum fructum auctori suo respondet. Hi quoque
pacifici, id est Christi discipuli, merito describuntur,
simul quia ipsi Ecclesiae fructus custodiunt,
vel malos foris doctrinae suae voce deterrent, vel suis
orationibus, de improbis canibus et bestiarum morsibus,
Ecclesiam quam Christus plantavit, defensare
non cessant.
chunks.english: “The thousand are yours, O Peaceful One, and two hundred belong to these.” If the twelve are multiplied by a hundred, they make twelve hundred. This number fittingly belongs to the apostolic men who, through the Gospel, have been spiritually begotten from the twelve in Christ. Established in the highest perfection, they answer their Maker like that best soil, by yielding a hundredfold fruit. These are also rightly described as peaceful people—that is, as Christ’s disciples—both because they guard the fruit of the Church, and because they either frighten away the evil people outside by the voice of their teaching, or, by their prayers, they never stop defending the Church planted by Christ from wicked dogs and from the bites of wild beasts.
chunks.notes: The interpretation links the twelve apostles with the hundredfold fruit of the good soil, producing the symbolic number twelve hundred.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
[Col. 0993B] Num. 198. Quae habitas in hortis. Quae redundas in
populis sub cultu justitiae constitutis, vel doctrinae
spiritualis aqua semper irriguis.
chunks.english: “You who dwell in the gardens.” That is: you who abound in peoples established under the cultivation of righteousness, or peoples always watered by the stream of spiritual teaching.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 199. Amice, ausculta, fac me audire. Dicit in
Evangelio Dominus discipulis suis: Jam non dicam
[Col. 0994A] vos servos, sed amicos (Joan. XXV) ; et iterum: Qui
habet sponsam sponsus est, amicus autem sponsi, qui
statim audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi
(Joan. III) . Fac me audire vocem tuam: illam utique
quam remunerandis fidelibus dicis: Euge, serve bone
et fidelis, quia super pauca fuisti fidelis, super multa
te constituam; intra in gaudium Domini tui (Matth.
XXVIII) .
chunks.english: “Friend, listen; let me hear you.” In the Gospel, the Lord says to his disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends,” in the Gospel of John, chapter twenty-five. And again: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and listens to him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice,” in the Gospel of John, chapter three. “Let me hear your voice”—that voice, surely, with which you speak when rewarding the faithful: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many. Enter into the joy of your Lord,” in the Gospel of Matthew, chapter twenty-eight.
chunks.notes: The printed text gives “John chapter twenty-five” and “Matthew chapter twenty-eight,” but the quotations are John chapter fifteen, verse fifteen, and Matthew chapter twenty-five, verse twenty-one. The phrase “statim audit eum” appears to be a scribal or printed error for “stat et audit eum,” “stands and listens to him,” matching John chapter three, verse twenty-nine.

chunks.speaker: narrator
chunks.latin:
Num. 200. Fuge, dilecte mi, assimilare capreae hinuloque
cervorum super montes aromatum. Qui conversatus
es nobiscum in terris, pronus regredere ad
superna. Sicque ascendens in excelsis, qui nunc appares
obtutibus carnis, adesto semper oculis cordis
ut te in fide retineamus quem aspectu non cernimus.
Assimilare capreae hinnuloque cervorum; quia tu es
[Col. 0994B] qui carnem suscepisti mortalium, et saltu celeri omnes
altitudines transcendisti coelorum. Super montes
aromatum, excelsior existens super omnem gloriam
angelorum.
chunks.english: “Flee, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” You who lived with us on earth, return eagerly to the heights above. And as you ascend on high—you who now appear to bodily eyes—be always present to the eyes of the heart, so that we may hold you by faith, though we do not see you by sight. “Be like a gazelle or a young stag,” because you are the one who took on the flesh of mortals and, with a swift leap, passed beyond all the heights of the heavens. “Upon the mountains of spices”: that is, you exist higher than all the glory of the angels.
chunks.notes: This closing interpretation reads the final verse of the Song as a prayer addressed to the risen and ascending Christ.
